titleFa: کتاب The God of Small Things
author: Arundhati Roy
introFa: کتاب «The God of Small Things» نوشته Arundhati Roy یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The God of Small Things»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 1 Introduction One of the glittering stars in the firmament of Indian fiction in English Arundhati Roy secured a very prestigious position not only in India but abroad also by dint of her excellence in art. She brought laurels to the country by winning the coveted Booker Prize in 1997 when India celebrated her 50th anniversary of independence. Roy has been first Indian woman who won this prize for her creations. She was born in Shillong in 1961 in Meghalaya to a Keralite Syrian Christian mother and a Bengali Hindu father, a tea planter by profession. Her mother, Mary Roy was well known social activist. Their conjugal lives were unhealthy and affected Roy badly. She said in an interview with Sunday Plus, “I don’t want to discuss my father. I don’t know him at all. I’ve only seen him a couple of times, that’s it”. Her mother was divorced. Roy spent a large part of her childhood in Ayemenem, a small town near Kottayam in Kerala, schooling in Corpus Christi. She left Kerla for Delhi at age of 16, and embarked on a homeless life style, staying in a small hut with the tin roof with in the walls of Delhi Feroz Shah Kotla. She proceeded to study architecture at Delhi School of Architecture; she is an omniscient writer and critic. She is master of style and technique. In an interview with India Today, Roy puts up things which throw much light on her determination and objectives of life: For practical reasons, I was terrified of place where I grew up, I knew I had to get away. I had to be economically independent; that’s the only way you can save your mind in India as a woman. The only thing that mattered to me was earning my own living at all costs. I knew I had to do a professional course, I was good at drawing and hopeless at math and in my second year of college I

was asked to leave home. (Newsweek, June 23, 1997:60) Arundhati Roy was awarded the Booker Prize for The God of Small Things in 1997. She won the National Film Award for best screenplay in 1989, for the screenplay of in which Annie Gives it Those Ones. In 2002, she won the Lannan foundation’s cultural freedom for her works about civil societies that are adversely affected the world’s most powerful government and corporation, in order to celebrate her life and her ongoing works in the struggle for Justice and Cultural diversity. Roy was awarded the Sydney Peace Prize in May 2004 for work in social campaigns and her advocacy of non-violence. In January 2006, she was awarded the Sahitya Akademi Award, a national award from India’s Accedemy of Letters, for her collection of essays on contemporary issues in her The Algebra of Infinite Justice but she declined to accept it in protest against the Indian government being violently and ruthlessly pursuing policies of brutalization of industrial workers increasing militarization and economic neo- liberalization. Arundhati Roy as an Indian English writer penetrates contemporary social-political issues which is amply perceptible in a number of articles, interviews and books. Various topics caught her attention like exploitation and oppression of deserted and woman corrupted system discriminatory attitude of the police and many social, political, psychological issues are well accommodated in her attempts and works. There is a nice blending of fact and fiction. In her praise Indira Nityanandan expresses a bit of her mind: Arundhati Roy writes in a style truly different from that of other Indo-English novelists both male and female of the country. She writes differently to great extent and in doing so breaks many of the accepted rules of language. There are passages in this novel where the technique override the content and one often has a feeling that the story gets stifled under the weight of her style. Her proclivity to experiment with language and its poetic attributes as well as her rapidly switching points of view, seeking to fuse the past and the present create difficulties in the ways of the readers, for long stretches the narrative appears to get bagged down while descriptions pile up. (Bhatt, Indira Nityanandan: 1999) From the lines mentioned above infer that she has strong adherence to liberty. Before 20th century, women’s writing were not accepted. The patriarchal culture never accepted woman’s artistic and social autonomy. In literary Paternity, Gilbert examines the metaphor of literary paternity, which defines authorship as a distinctly male act.

According to such a conceptualization of authorship, the text becomes a product or a child of the author/father, produced by the generation energy of the pen/penis (p. 188). Gilbert discloses that male author considers the female characters as his creations, men in general consider women as being created by from and for men (p. 194). Hopkins defines writing as a kind of male gifts and the paper on which he wrote as a metaphorical female womb (1986:188). The western civilization had always imagined the writer as the father of a text, just like God a assumed to be father of the world (pp. 188-89). The identification of the pen as a metaphorical pennies left many woman writers unsure of their right to write. I never let them be the model to be emulated. Despite it Jane Austen and Anne Frich faced the surges of the severe blow of the wind feeling emotional conflicts. They realized about them selves as abnormal/ criminals crossing boundaries (p. 191). They were made to believe that writing, reading and thinking are not only alien but also inimical to female characteristics (p. 191). At one place in his letter to Charlotte Bronte Robert Southey wrote Literature is not the business of woman’s life and it can not be (p. 191). The early women novelists accepted pseudonym so as to hide their identity. George Eliot wrote, like men and from the man’s point of view (Hudson: 134). Independently, value of woman is not accepted. Even that celebrated idea of women’s virtue can only be described as man’s greatest invention. Women are persuaded to identify themselves as Ciphers, whose value has no meaning in the disassociation with men. Such a view denied them the autonomy to formulate alternatives to the authority that has imprisoned them and kept them from attempting the pen (p. 195). The ability to follow her inner voice, rather than having a set of restrictive rules ingrained in her, has been an integral part of her accomplishment as an adult writer. Roy comments, when I write I never re-write a sentence because for me my thought and my writing are one thing. It is like breathing, I don’t re-breathe a breathe, etc. Arundhati Roy has been a screen writer and social worker, fought much for the welfare of the society. Her keen eyes are always ready to catch austere aspects of life and society. As an ardent journalist she became very popular among people. She raises her voice of protest time to time. She is much frank in expressing her ideas. Arundhati Roy is brilliant in creating most striking and appropriate images utilizing metaphor, personification, irony, etc. But she has created poetry in prose by her clever use of similes. She is simply outstanding and highly impressive. Roy’s Soviet Intervention in Afghanistan : Causes, Consequences and Indian Resposponse, is reminiscent of her two recent essay on Afghanistan, The Algebra of Infinite Justice and War in Peace

(October 2001), following the American military strikes on the Taliban ruled Afghanistan. In 1994, Roy wrote a scathing review of Shekar Kapur’s films , Bandit Queen based on Malasen’s Book, India’s Bandit Queen : The True Story of Phoolan Devi (1991). In this review titled, The Great Indian Rape Trick I and II, Roy charged Kapur with misrepresenting Devi’s real life experiences. This controversial review, which was Roy’s passionate intervention in local feminist debates, drew a good deal of media attention, and also involved her in ugly court cases. Arundhati Roy is much conscious regarding the size and theme of The God of Small Things. In the words of Roy, for me the structure of my story, the way it reveals itself was so important. I really took a lot of care in designing the structure of the story. Because for me the book is not about what happened but how what happened affected people? (p. 46) By her ardent skill of sketching the picture of the time and environment she presents post sixties India before us. Ayemenam becomes a transforming world in miniature that is torn in disseminations individual as well as collective, emotional as well as instinctive. Roy’s words force the reader to brood sincerely upon the concerns shown in her novel. Much attention is drawn to the caste consciousness and shameful treatment of society and treatment of society and family towards woman. Our constitution provides plenty of privilege to minorities and women but matter of fact is that all are not well implemented keeping vested interest of officials. In the name of lows their conditions are too powerful to challenge so what if they could not achieve that goals. The great reformer and thinker Mahatma Gandhi also advocates the uprooting of the age old social customs and belief. He lays emphasis on the equality and justice, and consistent, to great extent. Our social customs or conventions as shackles which need to be broken. Roy not only highlights what is beautiful in the East but what is abominable as well. The bane of the Indian caste system that ought to be discarded is being perpetuated. In The God of Small Things the caste prejudice eventually leads not only to the victimization of Velutha but the destruction of the family unit. In the opinion of many perceptive readers of the novel, The God of Small Things is characterized as an extraordinary act of imagination. Explaining the reason why Roy’s novel was chosen over the other Booker Contender Jason Cowley, one of the five 1997 Booker Judge said: The God of Small Things fulfils the highest demand of the art of fiction to see the world, not conventionally or habitually, but as if for the first time. Roy’s achievement and it is considerable, never to forget about the small things in life: The insects and flowers, winds, and water, the out cost and the despised, she deserved to

win. The works of Arundhati Roy are: The God of Small Things (1997), The End of Imagination (1998), The Cost of Living (1999), The Greater Common Good (1999). The Algebra of Infinite Justice (2002), (Collection of essays : The End of Imagination, The Greater Common Good (1999), Power Politics, The Ladies Have Feelings,) Power Politics (2001), War Talk (2003), An ordinary Person’s Guide Empire (2004), Introduction to 13 December, A Reader: The Starage Case of the Attack on the Indian Parliament (2006), The Shape of the Beast: Conversations with Arundhati Roy (2008), Listening to Grasshopper: Field Notes on Democracy (2009). Speeches, Essays, Interviews, documentary featuring the works of Arundhati Roy. Come September Transcript of speech on 18th Septemebr 2002 and conversation with Howardzinn. Arundhati Roy on India, Iraq, US Empire and Dissent Interviews on Democracy now. (Abridged Version of speech of the world social forum in Mumbai 16, January 2004). Tide? or Ivory Snow?, Public Power in the Age of Empire (16 August, 2004 speech in Sanfancisco). ABC Radio National Transcript of Sydney Peace Prize Lecture (with audio). The most cowardly War in History opening statement at the Iraq tribunal article dated 24 June, 2005. Pod cost of Arundhati Roy and Pankaj Mishra discussing India in the World at the Shanghai International literary festival. Arundhati Roy on Obama’s War, India and Why Democracy is the Biggest Scam in the World. In The Valley of the Tigens, Inter Vice with Ascent magazine on the Narmada valley. Arundhati Roy on the Human Costs of India’s Economic Growth, the view of Obama in New Delhi, and Escalating US Attacks in Af.... Pak Roy’s revolts are also perceptible in her work The End of Imagination. Her revolt is against the nuclearization in India and abroad. She satires on the arrogance and dominance of politics and above all the drawbacks of nuclear arms and ammunitions are placed. The book The End of Imagination opens with the apocalyptic vision of nuclear exposition tested at the Pokharan site on 11th May, 1998. Roy observes the sorrows of the people who were living around the place. They could not participate in the joy of BJ P members. In very clear way Roy puts up her blatant remark proving ourselves as causes of destruction in this way: If there is nuclear war, our foes will not be China or America or even each other. Our foe will be the earth herself. The very elements—the sky, the air, the land, the wind and water will all turn against us. Their wrath will be terrible our cities and forests, our fields and villages will burn for days. Rivers will turn to poison. The air will become fire. The wind will spread the flames.

When everything there is to burn has burned and fires die, smoke will rise and shut out the sun. The earth will be enveloped in darkness, there will be no day only interminable night. Temperature will drop to far below freezing and nuclear winter will set in, water will turn into toxic ice. Radioactive fall out will seen through the earth and contaminate ground water. Most living things animals and vegetable fish and fowl will die. Only rats and cockroaches will breed and multiply and combate with foraging relict human for what little food there is. (pp. 12-13) Roy has been true follower of Gandhiji. Like Gandhiji she strongly believes in his theory of truth and non-violence truly speaking. The atomic war will prove to be the most immoral, savage and barbaric. In nutshell, it can be said that Arundhati Roy is a great champion for the cause of peace and prosperity, integrations and harmony. The frankness and boldness of Roy reminds me of Taslima Nasrin, who in the preface of the book Lazza expresses her opinion: The disease of religious fundamentalism is not restricted to Bangladesh alone and it must be to fight at every turn for myself. I am not afraid of any challenge or threat to my life, will continue to write and protest persecution and discrimination. I am convinced that the only way of the fundamentalist forces can be stopped is fall of as who are secular and humanistic join together and fight their malignant influenced for one, will not be silenced, (pp. 9-10) Arundhati Roy has used the name of Kurtz Forkari Saipu, an Englishman who had gone native and who killed himself when his love was taken away by his parents. She also keeps Conrad’s impact upon herself, so, has absorbed one part of Conrad’s message in his long story, namely, that the western colonialist himself carried evil in his heart, especially in this case homosexuality. From Roy’s work it appears that Conrad is not much clear to her but she inclined to follow him. Her explanation shows much and makes much clear. She stuck the phrase a peg on which to hang her own view of Kerala Society. Roy got the idea of complex structure from Faulkner. Rushdie is enough to point in the direction of the kind of structure Roy has developed in The God once again, we shall narrow down our compass to Rushdie’s Midnight’s Children and present a sampling of the images and linguistic forms that have repretitions in The God of Small Things. There is gusto for voyeurism in both writers, Rushedie and Roy. Many things worthy to hide are presented plainly and openly. Here, in this reference, clear impact of Rushdie upon Roy is very clear need not to be proved. But Roy in her novel shows children’s concern on the side of Ammu. Main source of her novel is her personal experience. Ammu

is shown to be a victim of social convention and narrowmindness and a vigorous female starved of love and sex. Like Rushdie she portrays a negative one. Treatment of the mother-character in The God perhaps requires a reference to projection of this image by Roy’s predecessors. In Joyce’s work, the mother embodies religion and as such she is in opposition to the son’s skepticism. Joyce may have altered the biographical details in order to sharpen and dramatize the conflict. Stephen refuses his mother’s request to say prayers at her deathbed; afterwards he is filled with a sense of remorse which reverberates throughout Ulysses. On Arundhati Roy influence of Marquez is traced. It is perhaps too general to be illustrated clearly. His use of poetic mode in prose fiction and of complex plots in which memory plays a great role might have been in Roy’s mind when she drew the lines for The God of Small Things. Joyce influenced Faulkner, Joyce and Faulkner influenced Marquez, Joyce, Faulkner and Maruez influenced Rushdie- that is the probability. Rushdie admires very much all the writings of Marquez and continues: I think though, there isn’t a very close relationship other than that they are both books which have a political content. What I think is that the way of writing—which you find all over the world, Garcia Marquez is not the only one—is still relatively rare in the novel, and what tends to happen is that all the people who write like that get put in the same basket, (pp. 19-20) Most recently, Roy has been involved in protesting against the Narmada Project her article The Greater Common Good in frontline disparages a project that could force millions to abandon their homes in order to provide limited benefits to the limited number of people. The effects of Narmada development on the local rural economy and people and Roy’s indictment of the operation of the World Bank and generations of state and national government appears in essays like The Grater Common Good, Power Politics. In January 2000, she was arrested during a protest in the valley, and released two days later. The focus on these encounters in the British press illustrates the problematic elisions generated in media discourses that seek to define Roy’s interventions: For example, Madeline Bunting says in her feature for the Guardian, reviewing Roy decision to give up the glory trail as Booker Prize winning novelist for the role of India’s most prominent activist and dambuster, insists on seeing. Roy as single handedly scaring several western contractors of the huge Narmada project. (Bunting, 2001:25) Roy’s interventions are more obviously part of a matrix of diverse

local and international resistances to the project. Bunting reading relocates the motivation for Roy’s resistance within a more private line of rebellion passed from mother to daughter, from Mary Roy challenges to laws of inheritance in the Supreme Court to Arundhati Roy’s compaings in the Narmada. Roy got a support from Bhaskar Ghose, who was then the Director General of Doordarshan for giving her good help in writing plays for cinema. She is known for her life projecting the influence of rural background both on her life as well as in her work. Arundhati Roy was potentially influenced by modern western fiction. Four most likely influences that Roy think and give shape to her novel are James Joyce, William Faulkner, Gabriel Gracia Marquez and Salman Rushdie. Two of these authors have been clearly named by Roy; herself has said that she admires Salman Rushdie and it is unbelievable that she did read his works closely. Roy takes she her time exploring the past by means of the present. Her novels provide one more example of Faulkner’s influence upon Third World writers, his method of torturing a story— mangling it, coming at it round about after portentous detours and delays presumably strikes a chord in stratified, unevenly developed society that feel a shame and defeat in their history. I assume that Roy’s basic reading as a genuine influence has been Rushdie’s Midnight Children on which she tried out variation and here is very little in her novel of Joyce and Marquez that could not come via Rushdie novel. Roy has shown their piteable condition in the character of Ammu, who fails to find her own identity. She is always under pressure and control, and struggle for economic. Arundhati Roy, like Salman Rushdie and James Joyce, has liberally used similes. Her description of nature is superb just like a child she observes minutely and paints the narration with appropriate colours to create the required effect like she glorifies the nature in the paragraph furnished below: “May in Ayemenem is a hot, brooding month. The days are long and humid. The river shrinks and black crows gorge on bright mangoes in still, dustgreen trees. Red bananas ripen. Jackfruits burst. Dissolute bluebottles hum vacuously in the fruity air. Then they stun themselves against clear windowpanes and die, fatly baffled in the sun.” (p. 1) Arundhati Roy is insuperable as far as her sense of discrimination, as far as colours and language are concerned. She can create her own words to emphasize an appropriate, different shades and colours of which we are not aware of like dustgreen, wet-green and moss green but she proves her point. This shows outstanding capacity of the novelist. Even she has depicted light in different varying modulations

as the sun light is fractured by “their Trunks of tilting trees” (p. 306) and “glittering sun-shine” (p. 1) wedge of light (p. 219) and “bright parallelogram of barred sun-light on the floor.” (p. 268) not only light even she has differentiated the smells like sick sweet smell; old-food smell, sour-metal smell, sickled smell, smell of smoke, a sour forty smell of red ants, back inside smell, smell of fresh wood shavings, smell of pickles, and smell of lover’s skin, etc. Arundhati Roy is very remarkable as far as her oldfactory sense is concerned. She has been a generous of child and animal. She has outstanding command over coining new words. She has used similes and metaphors to create appropriate effect of place, person and event. Without the depiction of slum (filth and dirtiness) the presentation of the untouchable cannot be completed. Arundhati Roy has been criticized for her detailed writing of what could have been either avoided or minimised just to prove her point. In fact she has, like other Indian writers in English has taken liberty in describing spots and object at length particularly those which are filthy, dirty to Indians in India. No matter all descriptions throw realistic effect upon the reader despite it they are unwanted and unwelcomed. Children hung their bottoms over the edge and defecate directly the squelchy, sucking mud of the exposed river bed. The smaller ones left dribbling mustard streaks to find their own way down. Eventually, by evening the river would rouse itself to accept the day’s offerings and sludge off to the sea, leaving wavy lines of thick white scum in its wake. Upstream, clean mothers washed clothes and pots in unadulterated factory effluents. Arundhati Roy’s failure to give a national dimension to the story, the twins are said to have been born at the time of India’s humiliation at the hands of the Chinese forces, but the political allegory turns out to be a frail veneer. Occasional reference to political developments appears to be merely incidental or ornamental. Once again her work invites comparison with Rushdie’s Midnight Children. In the latter work, Rushdie sufficiently underlines the allegorical purpose. Saleem Sinai tumbled forth into the world at the precise instant of India’s arrival at independence. He says, “I had been mysteriously hand- cuffed to history, my destinies indissolubly chained to those of my county. For the next three decades, there was to be no escape”, (p. 3) As we proceed in our reading of the novel, we find the fate of Saleem Sinai inextricably linked up with that of the nation and the important events in the history of independent India intimately affect him and those of his generation; and conversely, the actions of Saleem and his fellow ‘midnight’s children’ actually form the destiny of modern India. Thus, Saleem Sinai of Rushdie’s conception of modem Indian history emerges as a representative of the midnight’s children.

Arundhati Roy has beautifully and effectively projected the plight of women in Indian society. It may be because we have patriarchal family system in most part of India that the women in India are treated as a second rate citizen. She faces injustice and oppression in androcentric society. From the very birth woman is under control and strict supervision of mother, father, brother during her childhood in parents house, then under her sons as a widow, out of house as a worker in the factory or an employee in the office. Her freedom and sexual abuse lend her into self insecurity, no rights in her own family at Ayemenem where she has no locus-standi. Arundhati Roy has successfully displayed falsehood conventional attitudes through Rahel’s symbolic actions who manages to survive in Delhi and New York among the male dominated society. The height of male dominance and authority over women has been the Bengali husband who offers his wife to his boss just for an ordinary favour. Arundhati Roy has taken up the issue of feminism to fight for their identity and economic and sexual freedom. But Ammu and Rahel both because of the circumstances avoid feminists struggle for self respect and liberty. They surrender to low, sexual pleasure and loneliness. There is no doubt that The God of Small Things is full of merit and is a high quality fiction. It has truly depicted the Kerala society, its political movements, degrading Syrian Christian society with selfishness obscurantism and intolerable dirtiness and filth. Arundhati Roy knows the sufferings and injustice in India and naturally sympathizes with dispossessed and suppressed people. She accordingly criticizes C.P.I. (M). And another quality of Arundhati Roy is jumping of the narratives from future to past or rather from present to the past is only to create pathos and irony which is simply not possible in straight simple narrations. In this mode of writing we already know the event whatever worst is going to happen, has already happened in the earlier chapters and the pathos or love has already created an imprint on our mind. Therefore, the chronological order, though staggered at places, has been advantageous at places, which at large has been a drawback in the novel. Her writing is certainly unique and as it is most economical and has an undercurrent of connotation. In this respect Arundhati Roy’s mode is perfectly original and insuperable in fiction. Her imagery is full of art. The deeper you go in it you find fresh images beautifully created in the text which are new, appropriate and exposing and may be termed as foundation and cornerstones of the mood of the novel. We may call the novel as tragically. A novel composed of memories painted colourfully by the painter, author artistically that is exposition of her complexes, joys and sorrows, disappointment and desires, fears and hopes. She has masterfully narrated her experiences in an

absorbing, gripping work of art. She has transformed even the disgusting matter into an universal appeal. All these qualities have made The God of Small Things a world class novel which holds our attention and control our emotions from the very beginning to the end, whereas we are not so definite about thrill, suspense and endings. Arundhati Roy herself has presented her views to justify herself in The God of Small Things. “The great stories are the ones you have heard and want to hear again. The ones you can enter anywhere and inhabit comfortably. They don’t deceive you with thrills and trick endings. They don’t surprise you with the unforeseen. They are as familiar as the house you live in or the smell of your lover’s skin. You know how they end, yet you listen as though you don’t. In the way that although you know that one day you will die, you live as though you won’t. In the Great Stories you know who lives, who dies, who finds love, who doesn’t. And yet you want to know again.” (p. 229), The God of Small Things has taken Arundhati Roy to greater heights and is a glorious achievement in Indian fiction in English. Marxism enters the story through the machinations of the local leader K.N.M. Pillai. The other characters associated with the ideology are—Chacko and Velutha. What creates problems for the critic is the status and quantum of the Marxist matter within the scope of the story and its theme. A writer, of course, should have the freedom to present this theme, or any other theme for the matter, in whatever light she/ he chooses. Like George Orwell in Animal Farm, she/he can take a wholly negative view of Marxism. But she/ he will be liable to criticism if such matter produces artistic fault: or, instead of arising out of the story, is added from outside, or if the balance is deliberately tilted through authorial pressure. It is agreed the Chacko is a fake Marxist, the Pillai is a political opportunist; it may also be conceded that the C.P.M. and its government did not adhere to the true Marxist principles. But the question is how much of the life of Pillai and the Marxist theory and its criticism included in the novel are strictly relevant to the plot and theme. When we re-examine the communist theme within the limits of the novel, we find that the theorizing about the success of the communist party in Kerala is immature and not strictly required. Similarly, lengthy information about not only K.N.M. Pillal’s life but also his family and his son is not relevant. Although the novel is evidently autobiographical, the author has declared/that “the characters in it are all fictional” and that the author has taken liberties only with the location of rivers, level crossings, churches and crematoria. It is also

true that even when the prototypes are easily recognized the names have been changed. Mary Roy appears simply as Ammo, her brother Isaac as Chacko and Arundhati Roy’s own brother as Estha. Now the questions arise: why is E.M.S. Namoodiripad mentioned by name? Why are false and misleading statements about his ancestral home particularly highlighted? Can a writer take such liberties with persons and fact which are more or less widely known among the public? Arundhati Roy has not provided a convincing answer to these questions. The idea of old communists serving as waiters in the newly built hotel also seems to be a calculated move. Arundhati Roy has explored issues related to subalternity and untouchability, especially the religious hypocrisy, poverty and corrupted system. As a social reformist she presents many illustrations laying the realities embedded in the society. By humour and irony she discloses very naked realities, which need changes, with naturalness. Her outlook to life is very close to Mulk Raj Anand, R.K. Narayan, Virginia Woolf, Mahesh Datta. Her satirical portrayal of the contemporary society, her psychological study of the isolated and deviated character, her new and original style containing many new devices as opposed to the traditional reading of things, etc. have exercised a great influence on the reader of literary flavours. If a reader goes through this book, he is charmed by many beautiful word and phrases, images and symbols, sometimes he is found to be baffled by some ungrammatical constructions, new coinages, unconventional rhythm and bizarre phrases. The style she invented smells the Indian soil. India Today in its cover story concludes: Arundhati Roy triumphed because unlike the others, she had the guts and the overwhelming talent to invent a new idiom and vocabulary to tell the story of a seemingly remote people. Mammachi Sophie Mol, Estha, Rahel, Ammu and Velutha will stay with us popping up once in a while to remind us of some eternal truth. For this new conception of form and style she may be placed next to the line of great innovations like D.H. Lawrence, Henry James, James Joyce, Ezra pound, T.S. Eliot, Virginia Woolf and Salman Rushdie. Arundhati Roy got the recognition of an ardent artist in the international arena when she bagged the Booker Prize for The God of Small Things in 1977. Her maiden novel is replete with various problems rooted in our society. She has brilliantly disclosed the realities. In one sentence I can say that her novel is in fact an eye- opener for the world of literature. She displayed a parade of her genuine capabilities in black and white and the book became the God

of Books on the New York Times best seller list for ten weeks, people not only India but abroad also highly praised for authentic style and artistic perfection. Bringing out the novel The God of Small Things she proved herself a novelist of different taste before the conventional novelists. Her novel makes a dawn of a new era in Indo-Anglian literature with her new artistic techniques and devices. Having been affected by the bright aspects of this book David Godwin came to India for getting Roy’s signature to publish the novel. Roy applauses the historic venture of David Gadwin in the acknowledge of The God of Small Thing: for taking that impulsive trip to India. For making the water part, the book was an instantaneous success and it surprised the literary world. Roy presents the different stages of her experiment with the novel in an interview: Writing The God of Small Things was a fictional way of making sense of the world I lived in and the novel was the technical key with which, I did it I didn’t have any drafts, because I didn’t write the novel from beginning to the end in a linear way, I could write something here something there, until the whole book emerged. That’s one of the reasons why I didn’t show anybody the book before it was finished. There was not anything to show. (When You Have Written a Book, 106) In the praise of Roy’s new style she met Miller, says on the other hand that the book uses languages in a way that is rare...very rarely do you get some one who can tear apart the rules and give you some thing fresh and not pretentious (Surendran, 247-48). Roy used nursery rhymes and many Malayalam words. The language of the novel is fresh and childlike. It is fresh because it has no parallel in the world of fiction. Dr. Gilliam Bear, Professor of English at Cambridge University and chairperson of Booker Prize Committee, praises The God of Small Things for: It’s linguistic inventiveness, its narrative power and its courage. It was willing to move its readers to embroil them in events they could not control. Book often crumble on a second reading. But Roy’s has strengthened. The brilliances of her narrative contrivance became more and more apparent. The idiom of her language refreshed the mind. And the sombre story that she told gripped the emotions. (Mandal, 31) Roy employs symbolism, paradox, and irony in her novel. Velutha is symbolic of black complexion, unsociability, muted voice and the oppressed section of society. There is manifestation of The God of Small Things and the God of big things Velutha is both the God of the small things and God of loss. Double standard of the family toward women is not a new thing but age-old. Accused of the same crime are

treated differently on the basis of gender. This problem is well furnished in the novel. She throws due light on the politics too and internal face of the politicians who enjoy the luxurious life only say highly and highly about the objectives of the party. But they meet the situations to do something as per their announcements they go back without thinking no odd giving much priority to their personal life. Showing devotion for duty as pretentious, Velutha becomes victim of such politics. Coming to Pillai for his help he knows all realities and finds that there is gulf of difference between Pillai saying and doing. Being a Marxist he could not be saved. Thus, we came across with Roy’s humanistic approach and secular outlook. She declares that women and untouchables are subordinated to the dominant culture of the male world. They are rendered as destitute even in this modern era. Story’s temporal setting shifts back and forth from 1969, when fraternal twins Rahel and Estha are seven years old, to 1993, when the twins are reunited at age 31. Much of the story is written in a view point sympathetic to the seven years old children. She can reel off the real state of the deserted children. Sometime due to parents children are destined to meet various hindrances making their life harder. Prominent facts of Kerala life that the novel captures is communism, the caste system, and the Keralite Syrian Christian way of life. The title of the present novel shows a revolt not because Velutha and Paravan had been called The God Small Things. Velutha is an ordinary young man from untouchables who did not fight any heroic wars, nor he did any Herculean task. He is penetrated as prey of social injustice because he had loved Ammu, who belonged to the higher caste. By customs and social norms she is never allowed even to touch untouchable having virtues. Aijaz Ahmad express his assessment of Roy’s novel: Velutha is the untouchable carpenter, the maker of little wonders in carved wood and thus The God of Small Things, whose tempestuous sexual encounter with Ammu, the upper caste woman, towards the end of the story violates all the love laws laid down by caste boundaries and the ideas of propriety as to who will love whom and how. (Ahmad, 1979:105). Another critic as Kate Millett also points out: When a system of power is thoroughly in command, it has scarcely a need to speak itself aloud. When its working is exposed and questioned it becomes not only subjected to discussion, but even to change. (Millet, 1970: 58) The God of Small Things is a remarkable indictment of patriarchy—

apathy, injustice and oppression faced by woman in the androcentric society. Woman is victimized everywhere: as a daughter in her parent’s house, as a wife in her husband’s house, as a worker in a factory or as an employee in an office, whether in India or America. There is no need to elaborate on these points or to cite examples from the text. The God of Small Things covers major issues of the feminism. In this novel implicit theme is search for identity and liberty. Ammu is a valiant fighter for these causes, though the options open to her in the male-dominated order are not viable at all. She grabs the first opportunity for escaping from the oppressive atmosphere of her parents’ house in Ayemenem and rushes into a loveless marriage. It is another thing that as a consequence of this step she actually finds herself out of the frying-pan into the fire. Roy has given sufficient room space to history and politics. In historical and political framework she manifested her novel The God of Small Things. The Indian history and politics shape its plot and meaning in variety of ways. Some of Roy’s commentary on the surface with jokes and snippets of wisdom are about political realities in India. For example, Roy’s novel attack the brutal, entrenched, and systematic oppression at work in Kerala exemplified by figures of power such as inspector Thomas Mathew. Roy is also critical of the hypocrisy and ruthlessness of the conventional, traditional moral code of Pappachi and Mammachi on the opposite side of the political fence, the Kerala communist party, at least the fraction represented by Comrade Pillai, is exposed to be much more concerned with personal ambition than with any notions of social justice. He speaks highly in public yet never put in his practice. He is self-centred, and shows his benevolence. In spite of her commentary on Indian history and politics, Roy evaluates the Indian post-colonial complex, or the cultural attitude of many Indians towards their former British rules. After Ammu class her father a wiper in Hindi for his blind devotion to the British, Chacko explains to the twins that they come from a family of Anglophiles, or lover of British culture, trapped outside their own history and unable to retrace their steps, and he goes on to say that they despise themselves because of this. A related inferiority complex is evident in the interactions between untouchable and touchable in Ayemenem. The issue of unsociability has appeared in highly polished manner. It can easily be caught as Roy’s sensibility towards marginalized. Mulk Raj Aanand’s Untouchable has well dealt with this issue. When critical comparisons are made remember, however, that the dominance of the culturally is hybrid. Indian novel in Europe and North America after the publication of Rushdie’s Midnights Children in 1981 has coincided,

as Arnab Chakladar has noted, both with the interests of the burgeoning field of post-colonial studies and with resurgence of interest in British Raj in the culture at large (Chakladar, 2000). A more recent, and rather less polemic analysis of cosmopolitan writing is made by Graham Huggan In the Past-colonial Exotic: Marketing the Margins, in which he agrees that links clearly exist between post coloniality as a global regime of value and a cosmopolitan industry (Huggan, 2001). As far as historical realism is concerned in The God of Small Things does not in any way run together to the thematic objective of the novel. It emerges to have been a part of Roy’s intention to cover the bare bones of the story with detail of historical realism. In the politics of literature and culture, we are now cognizant of the new historicist position that there is no trans-historical or universal human essence and that human subjectivity is constructed by culture codes which position and limit all of us in various and divided ways that there in no objectivity, that we experience that word in language, and that all our representation of the world, our readings of texts and of the past, are informed by our own historical positions, by the values and position that are rooted in them. (Newton, 1989) Roy’s keen (historical) experience of communism in Kerala has been subjectivized in her fictional construction, which in itself constitutes a conscious act that is essentially political and for psychological causes and consequences. In a sense, the novel presents a study of individual and social psychology. In this novel Ammu’s outbursts of vulgarity were astonishing and a short psychological observation. The God of Small Things can be read, then, as complex engagement with certain aspects of contemporary post-colonial theory via the formal strategies of the cosmopolitan novel. And where Roy reinforces Bhabha’s psychoanalytic focus and seems to endorse the potential of hybridity, this connection is particularly convincing. However, by relating Roy’s work so closely to accepted notions of post-colonial theory, Bhabha himself describes as the Enunciatory disorder in the writing of culture difference (Bhabha, 1994). Thus, in this chapter multi-faced personality of Arundhati Roy has been highlighted. By dint of her innovative style she has carved a new horizon to struggle. 2 Tenet of Realism and Romance This chapter poners over the tenets of Realism and Romance and their application in Arundhati Roy’s The God of Small Things. Her novel is replete with realism and romance. Before expounding its place in her novel realism’s and romance’s notion should be clear. Realism is an attitude describing life. To reproduce nature, in all its aspects as faithfully as possible, realism is employed in literature. It is based on the doctrine that is external perception, the objects immediately known are really in existence. So, it is the tendency to observe and represent things as they really are even in their most ignoble aspects. As such, it rejects three things: 1. It rejects the idealizing of reality in favours of beauty, 2. It is against representing thing according to a convention rather reality and 3. It rejects to deal with such subject matter as is transcendental and supernatural. Hence, there are three slogans of realism: Rely on reality, Represent reality, Avoid unreal or subjective. Realism is applied by literary critics in two diverse ways: 1. to identify a movement in the writing of novels during the nineteenth century that included Honore De Balzac in France, George Eliot in England, and William Dean Howells in America (see realistic novel under novel) and 2. to designate a recurrent mode, in various eras and literary forms, of representing human life and experience in literature. Realistic fiction is often opposed to romantic fiction. Realism

may be defined as the representation of reality of human life, incidents and characters. It depicts the real picture of life with its all colours. It heeds little to imagination or fantasy. It means, life is as shown as it is. In this reference, here, opinion of Merriam may be put up: Realism rejects imagination idealization in favour of close observation of outward appearance, realism in literature, theory or practice of fidelity to nature or to real life and to accurate representation without idealization of everyday life. (p. 1352) The concept of reality transmuted into art demanded verisimilitude and the delineation of man wholly into his physical setting. The novelist, thus, becomes a detached observer of contemporary society who provides the reader with a transparent window to reality. To the Victorian novelist, critic and reader, the correspondence of fiction to actual life became the central aim of literary creation. The aim of the realist author is to make the reader believe that what is being narrated is true, or has really happened; it reconstructs reality to give the semblance of the truth when readers get the theme and characters with spectacle derived from the real world. They attempt to find out similarity between theirs and characters of the creation. The classic realist’s text, thus, purports to instruct the reader by providing a detailed representation of daily life and ordinary life experiences. As it is mentioned that the realism stands for reality against romantic fiction very simply we can expound romance by saying that romance presents life as we would have it be more picturesque, fantastic, adventurous or heroic than actually: realism on the other hand, is said to represent life as it really is. This distinction in terms solely of subject matter, while relevant is clearly inadequate. Caranova, D.H. Lawrence and Winston Churchill were people in real life, but their biographies demonstrate that truth can be stranger than literary realism. It’s more useful to identify realism in terms of the effect on the reader. Realistic fiction is written to give the effect that it represents life in the social world as it seems to the common reader evoking the sense that its characters might in fact exist, and that such effects the novelists we identify as realists may or may not be selective in subject matter—although most of them prefer the common place and the everyday, represented in minute detail, over rarer aspects of life but they must render their materials in ways that make them seem to their readers the very stuff of ordinary experiences. For example Deniel Defoe in the early eighteen century dealt with the extraordinary adventures, a ship wrecked mariner named Robinson Crusoe and with the extraordinary misadventures of a woman named Moll Flanders; but he made his novels seem to readers a mirror held up of reality by his reportorial manner of rendering all the events,

whether ordinary or extraordinary in the same circumstantial matter of fact and seemingly unselective way. Both the fictions of Franz Kafka and the present day novels of magic realism achieve their effects in large part by exploiting a realistic manner in rendering events that are in themselves fantastic, absurd or flatly impossible. Jane Austen provided pictures of domestic life in country villages. Indeed, according to Ian Watt, the formal realism of the eighteenth century novel embodies the defining characteristics of the novel genre as a whole. George Eliot follows the stance to depict art as an attempt to interpret reality; she contends that if fiction should represent life in its highest complexity, the point of view in her novels should be multiple and shifting, seeing that any attempt to limit the representation of her novels was to focus on the ordinary lives of common people, and apart from the desire to portray rounded character she had the moral aim of promoting sympathy by extending knowledge and experience. She had an allegiance to the truth; and as the omniscient narrator presented the multiple perspectives of her characters to provide the knowledge necessary to interpret reality. The aim of nineteenth century writers was thus to reproduce pictures that shall impress by their close and truthful resemblance to something or there in real nature or life. In Adam Bede, George Eliot affirms that one of the important requirement of the novel was to enact the faithful representation of external reality; My strongest effort is to give a faithful account of men and things as they have mirrored themselves in my mind. However, she proceeds by acknowledging that the mirror of doubtless defective; the outlines will sometimes be disturbed; the reflection faint or confused. Nevertheless, Realist thought held the assumption that the role of the novelist was to be true to life and construct a comprehensible world in fiction. In the Art of Fiction, Henry Tames asserts that the air of reality is the supreme virtue of a novel the merit on which all its other merits helplessly and submissively depend. Indeed, the quest to convey the illusion of life, remained a concern with modern writers who shifted their concerns from objective realism to subjective realism. As Christopher Nash remarks, in a profound sense Realism and Modernism are devoted to the same and the retrieval, the recovery of that ultimate reality. Characters and incidents also depict the real and truthful things of life where realism is found. Pam Morris presents a bit of his mind: Events and people in the story are explicable in terms of natural causation without resort to the supernatural or divine intervention.

The scope and field of realism is too vast to define in few words. As far as types are concerned we can do nothing better than to quote the words of Bijay Kumar Das: If we take a look at the broad treads in Indian English fiction, we will be struck by realism that underlines this genre in the post- independence period. We come across five broad types of realism, social realism, psychological realism, historical realism, mythical realism and magical realism in Indian English fiction, (pp. 168-69) As far as romantic literature is concerned it was written in old French, Anglo-Norman and Occitan, later in English and German. During the early 13th century romances were increasingly written as prose. In later romances, particularly those of French origin, there is marked tendency to emphasize themes of courtly love, such as faithfulness in adversity. Early persecuted heroines were often driven from their husband’s home by the persecutions of their mother-in-law, whose motives are seldom delineated, and whose accusations are of the heroines having borne monstrous children, or committed infanticide, or practicing witchcraft or which appears in such fairy tales as The Girl without Hands and many others; but, as time progresses, a new persecutor appeared: a courtier who was rejected by the woman or whose ambition requires her removal, and who accuses her of adultery or high treason, motifs not duplicated in fairy tales. During the early 20th century romances were increasingly written as prose, and extensively amplified through cycles of continuation. These were collated is the vast, polymorphous manuscript witnesses comprising what in now known as the Valgate Cycle, with the romances of La Mart Le Roi Artu (c. 1230). Perhaps its final installment. In the Renaissance also, the romance genre was bitterly attacked as barbarous and silly by the humanists, who exalted Greek and Latin classics and classical forms, an attack that was not is that century very effective among the common readers. In England, romance continue; heavily rhetorical, they often had complex plots and high sentiments, such as in Robert Greene’s Pandosto (the source for William Shakespeare’s the Winter’s Tale) and Thomas Lodge’s Rosalynde (based on the medieval romance Gramelyn and the source for As You Like It). Arundhati Roy has moulded her novel The God of Small Things in the realistic and romantic framework. Through her art of characterization Roy brings out realism and romance. The God of Small Things has a number of characterization that they become alive among the readers. Almost all of the characters are realistically portrayed. They resemble the reader’s sentiments and some of them even arouse

their sense of pity and catharsis. The characters of the novel can be broadly divided into two groups—those who belong to the Ayemenem house, e.g., Pappachi, Mammachi, Baby Kochamma, Sophie Mol, Ammu, Rahel and Estha, and these who are outside the big house, e.g., Velutha, Vellya Pappen, Kuttapen, Muraleeddharan, K.N.M. Pillai, Inspector Thomas, etc. We can also democrat a line between these various characters on the basis of the two powerful symbols, Laltain and Mombati, employed by author. Former stands for the rural and later for ruled. Characters who denote Laltain are Mammachi, Pappachi, Baby Kochamma, Chacko, Inspector Thomas Mathew, etc., dominating over the Mombatties or the downtrodden of the book. Similarly, under the caption, mombatli we evaluate characters like Velutha, Ammu, Rahel, Estha. Ammu, is a tragic figure humiliated and misbehaved by her father, ill-treated and misbehaved by her husband, badly insulted by the police and deserted and rendered destitute by her brother. Her tragic story, right from the beginning to the end, arouses our sense of pity and catharsis. Like the tragic heroes of Shakespeare, she has to face so many trials and tribulations, cares and anxieties. She seems to disprove Aristotle’s conception that man of high ranks alone can have tragic grandeur. She also falsifies Bradley’s claims that Hamlet’s notion couldn’t have happened to a plumber. Though she has harboured in the core of her heart almost all the important virtues of a great character, but has one fatal flaw in her nature (like most of the tragic heroes of Shakespeare). The flaw which ultimately leads to her death is that she didn’t follow the age long rigid tradition of a patriarchal love laws that lay down who would be loved. And how. And how much? (p. 328). Before we analyze the various shades of Ammu’s character, we should known well at first the task of a novelist regarding portraying the picture of a great character. Roy helps us to discover some of the unfathomable depths of women character particularly in Ammu, who at times seems to identify her emotions to most of the common women we see in our day to day life. Similarly, whatever we see in the character of Ammu, has some relevance to our own attitude. Ammu generalizes other Indian women living in patriarchal society bound to live stinking lives, Ammu very aptly exposes the social reality and psychological also. Since childhood Ammu is forced to live tragic life. A child is supposed to lead a life free the encroachments of experience. Why? because a child’s world is the world of innocence, ignorance and simplicity. She must not be tortured by the tormenting experience of the grown up people. But the case of Ammu is somewhat different. In Roy’s terminology, she is a Mombatti of the big house, which is unable of face the surge of wind. As a little girl, Ammu had to endure some

unbearable nightmarish experiences. She saw with her open eyes the cruelty of her father, Pappachi, who used to beat her and her mother, Mammachi with a brass vase. Once it so happened that her father tore a pair of her shoes she had brought for herself. She was also deprived of the higher education because, according to Pappachi, college education is not at all useful for a girl. This shows the truthful portrayal of the women of the society who find nothing but a step motherly treatment in a male dominated family. Even her fundamental right to take education is deprived. The novelist depicts the cruelty and the schizophrenia of Pappachi in a very fine way. She says: not content with having beaten his wife and daughter, he tore down curtains, kicked furniture and smashed a table lamp. (p. 181) India is land of many diversity. On this earth it is woman who is held responsible for all actions. Without any ill-feeling all rights are snatched from them showing indifference for them. Roy has highlighted this reality, mostly girls having desire to take education, cannot get education and when they are not educated, no one can imagine them to emerge as a powerful agent who can destroy discrimination. Being successful in this persona they can be themselves make to obtain their right forcely. Manju Kapur’s character Virmati is recalled here, who also revolts against her own family to obtain education and get married but she fails. Some happens in case of Ammu, she also fights bitterly to break shackles of social conventions. But fact is that escape is not possible. Soon after the marriage, Ammu realized and found out she had jumped out of the frying pan into the fire. Her husband whom she loved so much proved to be an alcoholic who even made her smoke. At that time twins were born. Meanwhile Mr. Hollick, the English manager of the tea plant developed his weakness towards Ammu. Mad with the passion of sex one day he summoned her husband and asked him to resign the post. He become dumb founded to hear his resignation. Actually, the manager wanted to have the sexual relation with Ammu. He told: you are very lucky man, you know, wonderful family, beautiful children, such an attractive wife, (p. 42) He suggested that Ammu be sent to his bungalow to be looked after. Her husband put this proposal before his wife. This extreme humiliation created a sense of great hatred in the heart of Ammu. Roy has exposed very harsh picture of husband’s face. In a scuffle, she hits her husband with a heavy book and left the place with the twins Estha and Rahel. Ammu returned to Ayemenem with her pulled out cheeks, and there too, she found her parents cold and indifferent to her and her children. Her eyes welled up when she saw the miserable condition of the twins. She imagined her twins like a pair of bewildered frogs engrossed in each other’s company lolloping arms in arms down a

highway full of hurtling traffic (p. 43). The novelist flings a harsh irony on man’s domination over woman. She makes a home and when a home becomes not more than prison, it is a great shame without women, no one can think of home. Beauty, charm and all decoration of the house is women only so, in houses they should not be molested and humiliated. They need not to be worshipped but treated equally. She should be treated like human. A woman is generally more emotional, sensitive and tender, though she is also endowed with a greater power of patience and endurance. She can be viewed in numerous ways, but none of her facts is so overwhelming as the physical attraction she arouses for herself in the heart of the male sex. In this field of love and mating, she plays a role so exceedingly significant that the very basis of creation and procreation will come to a standstill. It is here we find her in the role of a beloved, a wife and a mother. She forms the pivot and nucleus of family life. Without the presence of the woman, home is not home but a dreary wilderness. This is exactly what Arundhati Roy wants to make us feel, see and behave the woman of society. But the Ammu has to see both in her husband’s house and her own house in Ayemenem is not based on the fair principle of equality. The author flings a harsh irony on the man’s domination over woman. Roy claims that women are not a mere toy or on object of pleasure or a means of gratifying the man’s baser passions but the noble and the richest part of man’s life and beautiful creation of the God. In absence of woman all beauties will be vanished. So, they should be safeguarded by all means. Ammu is step motherly treated in her own house. Her father didn’t believe that an Englishman, any Englishman, would covet another man’s wife (p. 42). Her brother Chacko used to fling irony on the twins and said that Estha and Rahel were indecently healthy. And so was Sophie Mol. He said it was was because they didn’t suffer from inbreeding like most other Syrian, Christians and Parsees: (p. 61). Ammu’s mother, Mammachi develops the same opinion. It is a great irony that a daughter estranged from the husband is tortured and tyrannized in the parent’s house. But on the other hand, an estranged son, Chacko, not only receives warm welcome but also remains the right inheritor of the family’s wealth and fortune. When he flirts with low-women, he is encouraged by Pappachi in the name of Man’s needs (p. 268). Whereas the same behaviour of Ammu is treated as illicit, untraditional and sinful: she is being locked in a room and is beaten black and blue. Mareover, the distant relatives came to see Ammu in order to show their sympathy. But actually, what they do was not sympathy but only they chuckled Ammu’s discomfiture whileout worldly they expressed their lip sympathy as a result, as Ammu

quickly learned to recognize and despise the ugly face of sympathy (p. 43). This shows inequality dwelled in her own house. Like other human beings she also aspires to be loved and cared but not allowed to do so. She spent hours on the riverbank with her little plastic transistor shaped like a tangerine. She smoked cigarettes and had midnight swim. In other words, at her home and in her family and the society, she became virtually untouchable, it can be obviously seen in the point of view of Baby Kochamma, The lady Macbeth of the novel. She said: A married daughter had no position in her parent’s home. As for a divorced daughter, she had no position anywhere at all. And as for a divorced daughter from a love marriage, well, words could not describe Baby Kochamma’s outrage. As for a divorced daughter from a intercommunity love marrigage Babay Kochamma chose to remain silent on the subject, (pp. 45-46). So the irony here is that women in this novel are against the women. Though Baby Kochamma had to pass through deep distress, still she doesn’t show sympathy to her own kin. This shows man’s psychology that is, when a man’s past is not happy, he wants to obtain the lost happiness by hook or crook. And if he fails to do so, he develops a sense of hatred to other person also and keep himself isolated. This is what we see here. But the real tragedy begins to take its toll when Ammu comes in contact with Velutha, a paravans untouchable of the village. Velutha belongs to an untouchable caste, as the novelist observes: Paravans were expected to crawl backwards with a broom, sweeping away their foot-prints so that Brahmins or Syrian Christians wouldn’t defile themselves by accidentally stepping into a paravan’s foot print, (p. 13) Ammu loved Velutha form her very childhood, but not so much for his exceptional talents but for his fiery spirit of protest. On her return to Ayemenem, one day she saw Velutha marching with a red flag in a white shirt and mundu with angry veins in his neck (pp. 11-12). Now the question is that why Ammu is drawn towards the fiery spirit of Velutha. Perhaps she wanted to identify her emotion of revolt with that of Velutha and search a shelter for herself. She loved Velutha heart and soul for his indomitable spirit of protest which she also nursed in her heart. She hoped that under his careful cloak of cheerfulness, he housed a living, smug, ordered world that she so raged against (p. 176). Moreover, while Velutha had held her daughter in his arms, she felt that he is not only the giver of gifts but she has also many gifts to give him. Lover and beloved are not generally accepted in our society.

Basically when they are out of their caste. So, such relationship carries no meaning. Well, this personal relationship between Ammu and Velutha leads them into illicit sexual relations now she smelled the river on him. This particular paravan smell that so disgusted Baby Kochamma. Ammu put out her tongue and tasted it, in the hollow of his throat. Caste subalternity is vividly portrayed through the life of Velutha in The God of Small Things. Velutha is being discriminated in the name of caste. Though he is an excellent worker in the factory, the co- workers do not like him. They are jealous of Velutha for his ability to carry out certain works with precision and accuracy. Velutha could not get any kind of mercy from the political party, police and finally the children. He was renounced by them all and nobody protested against Velutha’s death in the police custody. He stepped on to the path that led through the swap to the history house. He left no ripples in the water (p.289). Thus, Ammu is entirely tragic character tortured and abused by the police, family and politics. It is not the male folk alone responsible for her tragic plight but mostly the women characters like Mammachi and Baby Kochamma who may be called the real culprit to engender suffering in Ammus’s life. We may quote the famous observation of Luce Irigaray, a well known French feminist whose thought is quite applicable to Ammu: The relationship of women to their mothers and to other women thus towards themselves are rare total narcissistic black out, these relationship are completely devalued. Indeed, I have never come across a women who doesn’t suffer from the problem of not being able to resolve in harmony, in the present system, her relationship with her mother and with other women. Psychoanalysis has totally mythologized and censored the positive value of these relationship. In nutshell it can be described that Ammu’s character presents the picture of the average women character, we dig out three important diamonds. It is this powerful virtue, which makes her divorce her husband. Second, she has a great capacity to endure suffering upon sufferings. Third, she believes in the theory of etiquette and manner, decorum and decency. She never harbours in her heart any grudge against anybody. Arundhati Roy lashes out at the hypocritical moral code of society, which creates a gulf of difference between men and women. Fact that is a woman has a great place in the life of a man. If a man is a flower, the fragrance is women; if a man a ship, the radar is woman. She is prime in all sphere, without her life cannot be imagined. When she is source of life and giver of life, her life should
