3 Quest for Identity/Self This chapter deals with Arundhati Roy’s protagonist’s search for identity/self in her debut novel The God of Small Things. Identity is carved by ones and becomes his/her authentic recognition. There are two words: 1. living and 2. existence. Living denotes only breathing without any identity whereas existence shows real identity. This says, there is good to nothing in life. This stresses on the existentialism, a philosophical theory. Existentialism puts emphasis on essence which is particular identity. Roy has barely exposed many issues in the novel The God of Small Things. Being an activist she revolts against social discriminations and inequality of rights between man and woman. She realized, downtrodden has no right to carve their identities and keep it alone, their Gods live on the earth. The behest of their earthly master is more prime thing to follow than to fulfil their aims. They, without any protest, are willing to adhere with the orders and rules made by upper caste people. Velutha, who is paravan by birth has no right to think high about his career and cannot be supported by the upper caste people. On being talented he is not allowed to make any sign even on the sand. He is only living not exist. When we delve deeply in the character of Velutha, we get a spark of revolt but this seed is subdued. His dream is shattered and is insulted and much exploited at the hands of his own communist friend. Search for identity stealthy infilters in Velutha’s character. While living on the tea estate in Assam, Ammu declares her identity—and freedom through her manners and behaviour at social

gatherings. When her husband makes a most degrading proposal she meets violence with violence. At the Ayemenem House, she is constantly reminded that she and her children have no locus-standi; she nonetheless continues her struggle in her own way. She has the courage to taunt her brother Chacko about his hypocrisy and phallocentricism, and to move around in full independence. Rahel has equally grim odds to contend with. She displays her stamina by her actions. She indicates the falsehood of conventional attitudes through her symbolic actions already discussed. She manages to survive both in Delhi and New York in spite of oppressive male domination. When we begin to investigate the conduct of Ammu and Rahel further from the feminist point of view, problems begin to arise. One of the focuses of feminist thought is the emphasis on the biology of the female body from the woman’s point of view and not as an object of male desire. The notorious scene in Ammu’s bathroom is a case in point. Ammu carefully examines the parts of her body and seems to be appreciating the beauty of the female form per se. But soon after that, she weakens. She begins to be worried that her body will soon begin to loosen and she feels a suggestion of madness. She looks at her body- part as objects of male consumption, arid abandons their aesthetic form. The point to be emphasized here is that Ammu becomes reckless and runs into fierce pursuit of sexual satisfaction. She also takes the initiative in the actual act of sex but in this process she has left behind the true feminist objective of self-identity and sexual freedom. Feminists perhaps would hesitate to cite her as an example of true female. As for Rahel she survives the vicissitudes. Ultimately she resorts to a kind of happiness which would not be approved of from the feminist point of view. In this way Ammu and Rahel have avoided the proper cause of feminist struggle for self-respect and freedom. They ultimately conduct themselves to a state of degraded sexual pleasure and extreme loneliness. One of them destroys herself in her illusory pursuit of redemption. Her incestuous satisfaction promises no real break- through in the direction of feminist objectives. We now return to the description of love-making of Ammu and Velutha. The general pattern of events is not much different from what we find in modern western formulaic fact which seeks to find place for various kinds of sexual activities. Roy’s descriptions one almost pornographic and often descends to naked description. However, the description as composed by Roy constantly echoes with deeper and wider sentiments that involve larger issues and human considerations: in description of love making of Ammu and Valuetha and Mammachi i’s magnification of their manner of loving

each other, pornography is reflected. Once he was inside her fear was derailed and biology took over. The cost of living climbed to unaffordable heights; though later, Baby Kochamma would say it was a small price to pay. There are also crucial feminist ideas to reckon with in this account of the sex act. For one thing, we have already drawn attention to the active role of Ammu in the whole proceedings—the woman claims her right as an equal partner. Equally important is the right of woman to secure her full delight, which is bound to be delayed owing to the age-old suppression of the organ on which proper sexual satisfaction for the woman actually depends. In the sexual act between Ammu and Velutha the lack of coincidence is highlighted and, what is more important from the feminist point of view, the woman insists on being fully satisfied. In view of what we have said above, it would appear simplistic to brand the description as a piece of unashamed pornography. Its deeper implications ought not to be set aside because its poetry and its feminist contention help to raise it from the level of mere sensationalization of sex and its crude description in terms of literal facts of the genitalia and their stimulation and behaviour during the act. Shobhaa De believes in the fulfilment of women’s biological needs equally. She advocates the night to be delight without caring of the conventions. She never poses herself against the marriage but she does not let marriage destroy all the pleasure of views. The God of Small Things sets forth quest of Ammu, Rahel, Estha. They are constantly struggling for their identities in the society. The novelist raises her own voice against the injustice of the characters mentioned above both by their families and society. Ammu aspires to be educated breaking the patriarchal rules to get her own identity. She also advocates right of education to girls. In the society boy’s education gets much importance but girl’s is not heeded. Roy indirectly puts this question before the readers whether without girl’s education our edifice can be erected. Too much sure, answer will be no knowing all drawbacks we never come forward to bring the change in the social structure. Every body has right to follow the path his/her own way. This is the right by birth. Brooding upon the consequence of Ammu’s struggle one should not give up the idea to protest against unlawful doctrines and structure from the feministic point of view. The God of Small Thing is superb novel presenting the real status of woman not only in the society but in her own house. Gynocriticism stresses much emphasis on women; it resulted in the need for creating a new language. One cause of this discrimination is language created by the male chauvinistic world. As a result, it is difficult for women to represent some of the male gender terms. In

Malayalam, there is no equivalent male gender term for Veshya which means a prostitute. In one of her interview with Gita Hiranyan, Sara Joseph says, if there is gender discrimination in the society there will be a language which denotes that discrimination (p. 102). The existing structure of the language needs to be dismantled so as to undermine the power within the male gender. The difference in women writing is the first step towards the dilapidation of patriarchal ideologies. Ammu, a female is step-motherly treated. In fact, even today though in spite of a fundamental improvement in woman’s position by our constitution and various amendments, we see in India, expect a fistful section of society, that the conservative and superstitious mind of a large number of people can be clearly seen in a conservative family where Purdhah is strictly maintained and also in the rural folks where women are supposed to be meant for only mating and procreating, serving and nourishing. Meena Usmani in her article Violence Against Woman rightly remarks: The women have frequently been ruthlessly exploited in our society and the problem is growing day by day. The case of eve- teasing, sexual harassment, abduction, sati, rape and wife battering in public and at the workplace, etc., have been more regularly reported since the 1960s and early 1970s. The issue of violence against women has become the public problem as the women are discriminated at work, home and are denied their due in every field. The constitution of India promises freedom, equality, opportunity and protection to women and give them several rights. In spite of that they enjoy an unequal status. (Meena, Usmani, p. 13) In an atmosphere entirely different, she began to feel like a captive in the big Ayemenem House. She had to help her mother in house work. So, she became the victim of frustration due to the sudden disruption of education, uncongenial atmosphere and an antipathy attitude of the family members. She wanted to fly freely in the sky of liberty. So, Ammu pays a visit to Calcutta, there, in someone’s wedding reception she happens to meet her future husband who was on vacation from his job. He was an Assistant Manager of a tea estate in Assam. But soon after the marriage, Ammu discovered that she had jumped out of the frying pan into the fire. At that time the twins were born, meanwhile Mr. HoUick, the English manager of the tea plant develops his weakness towards Ammu. Actually, the manager seeks to have the sexual relation with Ammu. Her husband puts this proposal before his wife. This extreme humiliation created a sense of great hatred in the heart of Ammu. This result is not of Ammu but of many females, who struggle for identity. Through Ammu, Arundhati Roy, a

great champion of the cause of women, here raises a number of questions on our age long myths and traditions, history and legends. She shows that right from the beginning of creation, woman have been the subject to many insults and abuses and also shows that women suffered much for their identity. But the bitter tragedy begins to take its toll when Ammu comes in contact with Velutha, a paravan untouchable caste, as Roy has written in The God of Small Things, Roy expresses: Paravans were expected to cruel backwards with a broom, sweeping their foot prints so that Brahmins or Syrian Christian wouldn’t defile themselves by accidentally stepping into a paravan’s foot print, (p. 73) The bond between Ammu and Velutha was maintaining since childhood. On Ammu’s return to Ayemenem, one day she sees Velutha marching with red flag in a white mundu with angry veins in his neck (pp. 71-72). They fall in love with each other. Arundhati Roy develops his character to the level of a tragic hero who suffers and attains tragic grandeur; his tragic death arouses a sense of pity and catharsis in the readers. The author calls him The God of Loss. What Edwin Muir observes about a dramatic figure can be mostly applicable to Velutha? He observes: The dramatic figure is the opposite of the man of habit; he is the permanent exception. He breaks habit, or has it broken for him; he discovers the truth about himself, or in other words develops. He dramatizes his real nature, where the fiat character dramatizes his second nature or at best something in him which has been real but is so longer, (p. 142) Velutha is an expert mechanic and craftsman. He was 14 when John Klein, a carpenter from a carpenter’s guild in Bavaria, came to Kottayam. It is he who taught the art of carpentry to Velutha. Every afternoon, after school, Velutha caught a bus to Kottayam, where he worked with Klein till dusk. At the age of sixteen, he finished his highs school and became an accomplished carpenter. He developed a German design sensibility (p. 75). The novelist observes: He built Mammachi a dinning table with twelve dinning chairs in rosewood and a traditional Bavarian chaise louge in lighter jack. For Baby Kochamma’s annual nativity plays he made her a stack of wire-framed angel’s wings that fitted on to children’s backs like knapsacks, cardboard clouds for the Angel Gabriel to appear between, and a dismantleable manager for Christ to be born in. When her garden Cherub’s silver are dried up inexplicably, it was Dr. Velutha, who fixed its bladder for her (p. 75). Apart from the skill of carpentry, Velutha has a special knowledge of repairing machines like radios,

clocks, and water-pumps. It is he who looked after the plumbing of all the electrical things in the Big Ayemenem house. Mammachi often said, if only he hadn’t been a paravan, he might have become an engineer (p. 75). Moreover when Mammachi decided to enclose the back verandah it was Velutha who designed and built the sliding- folding door that later became all the rage in Ayemenem (p. 75). He also oiled the water pump and the small diesel generator. Velutha has strong sense of uplifting from bottom to top. His father on the other hand, is a traditional, conservative man who wants to lead a life of untouchable only. Velutha, along with a number of dalit untouchables converts himself into the Christian religion only to immune from the victimization of a casteist society. But his conversion and his technical expertise, apart from many other good things, never bring any fruitful result in this callous society. Velutha, along with his father, always goes to the Ayemenem house to deliver coconut plucked from the trees. But they are never allowed to enter the room. They were not permitted to touch a thing that a Touchable touched. Mammachi remembers the days: When paravans were expected to crawl backward with a broom, sweeping away their foot-prints so that Brahmin and Christians wouldn’t defile themselves by accidentally stepping into a paravan’s foot-print. In Mammachi time, paravans, like other untouchables were not allowed to walk on public roads, not allowed to cover their upper bodies, not allowed to carry umbrellas. They had to put their hands over their mouths when they spoke to divert their polluted breath away from those whom they addressed, (pp. 72-74) Thus, Velutha has to undergo so many insults and abuses engendered by police, politics and society. Here the character of Velutha is very near to Bakha in the novel, untouchable. Bakha has to suffer insult and abuse without any rhyme or reason. He suffers only because he is an untouchable. In a fit of anger he bursts out: Why are we always abused? The sanitary inspector that day abused my father. They always abuse us. Because we are sweepers. Because we touch dung. They hate dung. I hate it too. But the basic difference between Bakha and Velutha is that the former is more active and aggressive than the latter. Velutha never believes in a frontal attack. He is a man of sober nature and congenial behaviour. But Bakha, on the other hand, always strives to raise hail and fire (though he doesn’t do it) on the high, caste people. M.R. Anand observes: But there was smoldering rage in his soul. His feeling would rise like spurts of smoke from a half smothered fire in a fitful jerks when the recollection of abuse or insult he had suffered kindled a

spark in the ashes of remorse inside him. (p. 58) But such emotions full of rage and anger do not find any place in the character of Velutha. He is a silent sufferer. He never behaves like a fuming and a roaring tiger; never tries to hammer the age-old norms of society and tradition; never behaves like a rough and savage man, a man who has nothing to do with etiquette and manner, decorum and decency. He is a man of innocence and ignorance. But unfortunately, this innocence is badly caught in the web of casteist mentality and the corrupt police administration. Though Velutha is a great carpenter and a skilled mechanic, still he does not command respect in society. His father is dead against any type of education or advance knowledge in a paravan. He thinks that in a paravan they could (and would and should) be construed as insolence. Further, Velllya quickly degenerates into nagging and bickering and consequently there is a sense of unpleasantness between the father and the son. In course of time, Velutha begins to avoid going home. He works late, catches fish in the river and cooks it in an open fire. He also spends the night out doors. All of a sudden, he is not seen for at least five months. He does not say anybody about his exile. When he comes to Ayemenem, Mammachi again rehires him as the factory carpenter and the general maintenance of the whole factory is given charge to him. But this causes a great stir in the factory workers. Why? Because the touchable workers of the factory are so wild with casteism that they think that the Paravans are not meant to be carpenters. So, in order to keep the workers happy, Mammachi pays Velutha lesser than she would give to touchable workers. M. Adhikari holds the view: In Velutha’s case it is class and taste discrimination that makes him powerless and not his gender. His greatest crime is that while being a kama he has dreamt of Draupadi (p. 46). Ammu is locked up in a room. Mammachi thought: She (Ammu) had defiled generations of breeding and brought the family to its knees. For generations to come, forever now, people would point at them at weddings and funerals, at baptism and birthday parties (p. 258). So, no sympathy, no support from anywhere, Ammu left the big Ayemenem House and died in a grimy room in the Bharat Lodge in Alleppey, where she had gone for a job interview as some one’s secretary. Thus, Ammu is an entirely tragic character tortured and abused by the police, family and politics and suffered much for her identity. She suffers mental crisis in her struggle of getting new horizon for her struggle. Ammu fights for her relationship with Velutha invented by herself. Being defiant she goes to the police station; she is called a vesya by inspector Thoman Mathew. Velutha is severely beaten by the police incharge with the alleged murder of Sophie Mol, though she is

naturally drowned in the river while playing on the boat. The police beat Velutha so mercilessly that he has to die in the custody. Arundhati Roy presents a heart rending pathos in describing the piteous plight of this untouchable: Blood spilled from his skull like a secret. His face was swollen and his head looked like a pumpkin, too large and heavy for the slender stem it grew from. A pumpkin with a monstrous upside down smile. Police boots stepped back from the rim of pool of urine spreading from him, the bright bare electric bulb reflected in it. (pp. 319-20) This shows dilapidation of Velutha’s and Ammu’s struggle for identities. Thus we see that Velutha, the untouchable, doesn’t sweep off his footprints are erased by the establishments -the police, state and tradition. Patriarchy and social custom punish both - the woman who has defiled generation of breeding (p. 258) and the paravans who has challenged the age long tradition of social morality. Both these Mombatties got punishment for unacknowledged fear—civilization’s fear of nature, men’s fear of women, power’s fear of powerlessness (p. 308). Laxmi Parasuram points out: Velutha’s place in history was predetermined, he was not expected to see many things, that were not of bounds for him, obscured by history’s blinkers. He was the God of Loss, The God of Small Things, of Goose Bumps and sudden smiles who had to go about furtively denying his own presence. But one day changed the whole course of his life; he was caught in the noose of history with a suddenness, which the big brought upon the small. In short, Velutha, the silent sufferer, takes no cognizance of social convention and restrictions and thus comes in conflict with history, administration and social code of conduct. Roy has so beautifully portrayed his character that the readers are very soon drawn towards him, that his tragic fall arouses an atmosphere of pity and catharsis in the mind of the readers. Next come to Rahel, one of twins of Ammu. She suffers much for her identity like her mother. Rahel is a child of broken home and daughter of a divorced mother absolutely neglected by the Ayemenem house. She is devoid of love and affection that a child is supposed to get during his/her childhood. Roy’s presents some beautiful episodes in Rahel’s childhood which clearly shows her rebellious and somewhat abnormal nature in order to search identity. At first, she is blacklisted

in Nazareth Convent at age of eleven when she was caught outside her house mistress’ garden gate decorating a knob of fresh cowdung with small flowers. The next morning she is made to look up the word depravity in the Oxford dictionary. Six months later she was expelled from the school after repeated complaints from senior girls. Roy observes: She was accused (quite rightly of hiding behind doors and deliberately colliding with her seniors). When she was questioned by the principal about her behaviour (cooled, coned, starved), she eventually admitted that she had done it to find out whether breasts hurt. In that Christian institution breasts were not acknowledged. They weren’t supposed to exist, and if they didn’t, could they hurt? (p. 16) Moreover, she also caught smoking. The other abnormal nature which she exhibits in school is setting fire to her housemistress’s false hair burn, which under duress, she confessed to have stolen. The teacher notes two important things. First, she is extremely polite child. Second, she has no friend. It is to be noted that the abnormalities we see in the character of Rahel is rooted to her past days. It is trauma that makes Rahel a girl of taciturnity, who always wants to lead a life far from the din and bustle of crowded city. Rahel is divorced like her mother Ammu After the divorce, Rahel works far a few months as waitress in an Indian restaurant in New York. After divorce Rahel comes to Ayemenem like her mother. We notice that she develops a casual attitude to life. Thus, we see that Rahel is a loving female character in novel. Right from her birth, she has been the sufferer of undeserved despair and desolation and has been a victim of the Pappachi’s moth which tormented every house that she ever lived in. As Mammachi is one of the prominent character in the novel, Mammachi, though not frustrated in love like Baby Kochamma, is an unhappy character in the book. She is also a sufferer of feminism and much for her identity. Her marriage life is not peaceful; she is a doll in the hands of her husband, Pappachi who used to beat her with an iron flower vase, only to show his patriarchal domination over a docile, submissive, ungrudging, unprotesting wife. In the very beginning, Roy presents a very pathetic picture of her life. She observes: Mammachi was almost blind and always wore dark glasses when she went out of the house. Her tears tickled down from behind them, and trembled along her jaw like raindrops on the edge of a roof. She looked small and ill in her crisps off-white sari. Chacko was Mammachi’s only son. Her own grief grieved her. His devastated her. (p. 5)

The frustrated and unsatisfied marriage of Mammachi shows the reader a different tale of woe. Thus both Mammachi and Baby Kochamma play the rules of villain in the book there is a minute difference between their respective fabrications. And both suffered much for their identity. One other character is Margaret Kochamma. She is the wife of Chacko and the mother of Sophie Mol. Like the other Mombattis of the book, she also suffers and loses her dreams in this male dominated society. After the marriage with Chacko, her life becomes more frightful and more insecure than before. A chain of misfortunes make her life sad and gloom, e.g., she gets a divorce; Joe, her second husband, dies; Sophie Mol, her dear daughter, also gets an unexpected death. Margaret Kochamma was working as waitress in a cafe in London when at first, she met Chacko, like Ammu, she left the house of her parents for no greater reason than a youthful assertion of independence (p. 240). Well, both Chacko and Margaret Kochamma were married without their family consent, without their family knowledge. But this untraditional rebellious marriage, as bad luck would have it, did not prosper in a fruitful way: Along with the pressured of living together came penury. There was no longer any scholarship money, and there was the full rent of the flat to be paid (p. 247). Moreover, she also grew fed up with the untidy, clumsy and undisciplined living of Chacko. To crown the effect, Margaret Kochamma’s parents refused to see her. Her father disliked Indians. So, very soon, she divorced Chacko and got herself married with Joe, a biologist. The author observes: Joe was everything that Chacko was not. Steady. Solvent. Thin, Margaret Kochamma found herself drawn towards a wedge of light (p. 248). Hence, Margaret Kochamma is a tragic character partly tortured by the powerful fate but mostly harassed and divested by her own fickle mind and in adapted conduct and in this way she suffered a lot for her identity. Thus, having discussed the quest for identity in case of Ammu, Velutha, Rahel, etc., we get one thing that transgression of age-old result is not easy task. Sometimes strugglers are badly trapped in the old and hardly breakable trap. Ammu is sense of revolt and aspiration to get her own identity recalls Manju Kapur’s female protagonist named Virmati and Velutha, Mr. Anand’s male character in untouchable Bhakha. 4 Psychological Realism in Roy’s Novel This chapter is to explore aspects revealing psychological realism in The God of Small Things. Roy has very ardently revealed the inner atmosphere of humans, especially women and marginalized. Plight of concerning creatures badly throws impact upon her thinking and doing. Roy is considered as an activist and art has paved way for activism in Roy. Thus, she raised her bold voice against the corrupted system. Frankly, it can be declared that Roy is champion of feminism. R.S. Sharma and S.B. Talwar think that there are unmistakable clues in the text itself which suggest that the reader pays some attention to the psychological aspects of the narrative. The plot and characterization reel off psychological reasons and consequences. In a sense, the novel The God of Small things presents a study of individual and social psychology. I find the characters themselves keenly conscious of the psychological forces in their family history and in their personality. After perusal of The God of Small Things it is found that Ammu and Velutha two characters are much suffered from the mental crisis and tortures of society. The autobiographical elements predominate in the novel. To great extent we get reflection of Arundhati Roy in her character Rahel. The present novel is superb blend of fiction and reality. With this novel the novelist’s leitmotif is to change the mental framework of the people especially readers. What is realized throughout her life is revealed. She was proposed to convert this novel into a film. But she rejected saying, filmmakers would infuse the book with their own imagination. My book belongs to its readers (Dhawan, 16). Her art of revealing or expressing the reality—sociological, psychological and historical is beyond any comment. Gender discrimination is burning issue. Man and woman are treated differently. Regarding education boys get all

facilities and opportunities which girls cannot get equally. Whereas education in society must be given to both men and women without any gender discrimination. Education develops all the faculities. So, keeping the benefit in mind of taking higher education. But what we find in this novel is somewhat different. Here, female character Ammu was not allowed to pursue education; but on the other hand, Chacko, her brother, is sent to Oxford to study further, though he is not better than his sister in anyway. In spite of this, Chacko is allowed to study further because he is a male-member. But Ammu, being daughter, is step-motherly treated. The double standard of the society towards women is revealed through Ammu’s family. Chacko is appreciated. Mammachi often said that Chacko was easily one of the cleverest man in India (p. 55). At this remark Ammu would say on what bases? (Ibid.) . Mammachi loved to tell the story (Chacko’s story) of how one of the dons at Oxford had said that in his opinion, Chacko was brilliant, and made of prime ministerial material (Ibid.). It shows that Ammu tries to spark revolt against such inequality. She does so but not supported by her family. She suffers from psychological crisis. She never agrees with the point that getting education from Oxford Chacko could prove himself better. Very proudly Chacko airs high (p. 41). He said, what’s yours is mine and what’s mine is also mine (p. 57). Here the author shows the psychology of the parents of conservative family that women should not be treated as men. Roy elucidates the cruelty and the schizophrenia of Pappachi in a very fine way. Roy says: Not content with having beaten his wife and daughter, he tore down curtains, kicked furniture and smashed a table lamp. (p. 181) From beginning to end Ammu feels as victim being crushed by her family and social norms. She is captured in her own house, and all her family members are against her. Her whimsicality throws her in arduous situation. In an atmosphere entirely different, she begins to feel like a captive in the big Ayemenem House from where escape is impossible. She has to help her mother in house work. So she gets frustrated and isolated. She desires to fly freely in the sky of liberty. Her wings fluttered: All day she dreamed of escaping from Ayemenem and the clutches of her ill-tempered father and bitter, long suffering mother. She hatched several wretched little plans eventually one worked. Pappachi agreed to let her spend the summer with distant aunt who lived in Calcutta, (pp. 38-39) Gender discrimination is revealed in The God of Small Things. Its pangs force character to brood upon their plight and condition. Ammu

many times is got lost in her dream. She is well acquainted with the fact that not a single mistake could be forgotten. While all other faults and mistakes of Chacko have no meaning for Mammachi and Pappachi is that he is their son. The throes of Ammu are elucidated through her monologue. This monologue expresses the psychological reality and along with we get the real knowledge of personality. Chacko and Ammu are severe and relentless. Ammu’s intercaste marriage could not be accepted but Chacko’s accepted. In one sentence it can be stated that Chacko is accepted with his faults by his family and society all times by all means. At the age of twenty-four, an age of enjoyment and merriment, Ammu’s life came to standstill. She spoke to no one. She spent hours on the riverbank with her little plastic transistor shaped like a transgenic. She smokes cigarettes and had midnight swim (p. 44). In other words, at her home and in her family and the society, she became virtually untouchable. It can be apparently seen in the point of view of Baby Kochamma, Lady Macbeth of the novel, she said: A married daughter had no position in her parent’s home. As far a divorced daughter, she had no position anywhere at all. And as for a divorced daughter from a love-marriage, well, words could not describe Baby Kochamma’s outrage. As for a divorced daughter from a intercommunity love marriage—Baby Kochamma chase to remain silent on the subject, (pp. 45-46) So the irony here is that women in this novel are against the women. Baby Kochamma had to pass through deep distress; still she doesn’t show sympathy to her own kin. This exposes man’s psychology—that is, when a man’s past is not happy, he wants to obtain the lost happiness by hook or crook. And if he fails to do so, he develops a sense of hatred to other person also. Ammu drifts towards a paravan knowing all reality in wake of his position in the society. But, constantly, she realizes huge void in her life, and when she castes sight on her twins, it fills her heart with agony and frustration. In this reference Roy reveals lots of psychological realities. Because of her dire need of love and security she starts to like and love even in her dream. Ammu loved a paravan and this unorthodox relationship initiated troubles for Ammu and Velutha. It was Mammachi, who retaliated first against Ammu for the forbidden relationship with an untouchable. She was worried about the society and a bad name that would be attached to her family for generations to come. In a patriarchal society, women’s choice has no value and they are bound to accept the general stream of life. Chacko commits a mortal sin by exploiting the poor women of the country,

but he is readily pardoned by Mammachi. On the other hand, a venial sin committed by her daughter Ammu was treated with a lot of contempt: Her tolerance of Men’s Needs as far as her son was concerned, became the fuel for her unmanageable fury at her daughter. She had defiled generations of breeding (The little blessed one, blessed personality by the patriarch of Antioch, an imperial Entomologist a Rhodes Scholar from Oxford) and brought the family to its knees. For generations to come, forever now, people would point of them at weddings and funerals. At baptisms and birthday parties. They’d nudge and whisper. It was all finished now. (p. 258) The real tragedy starts take its toll when Ammu comes in contact with Velutha, a paravan untouchable. An untouchable’s affair with a touchable woman is not granted in rural India, in any community. Even untouchable wouldn’t dare to do such things because they know the consequences. Ammu’s loved Velutha since her very childhood, but not so much for his exceptional talents but for his fiery spirit of protest. Well, this relationship between Ammu and Velutha leads them into illicit sexual relation. Now, she smelled the river on him. She felt her dream, her afternoon more move inside her like a rib of water rising from the ocean gathering into a wave. The cheerful one armed man with salty skin and as shoulder that ended abruptly like a cliff emerged from the shadows of the jagged beach and walked towards her (p. 330). Ammu longs for him and ached for him with the whole of her biology. Her particular paravan smell that so disgusted Baby Kochamma. Ammu put out her tongue and tasted it, in the hollow of his throat. She pulled his head down towards her and kissed his mouth (p. 335). But this happy moment does not last long. One day, Vellya Papern, Velutha’s father, secretly sees their love making and so, he broke the news to Baby Kochamma; consequently, Ammu is locked up in a room. Mammachi thought: She [Ammu] had defiled generations of breeding and brought the family to its knees for generations to come, forever now, people would point at them at wedding and funerals at baptism and birthday parties, (p. 258) Lines above mentioned present psychological concern of Mammachi. Such many instances are exposed only by mental operation of the characters which reveal the reality. So, no support, no sympathy from anywhere, Ammu left his Ayemenem House and died, in a grimy room in the Bhart Lodge in Alleppey, where she had gone for a job interview as some one’s

secretary. She died alone (p. 161). Hence, Ammu is ill-treated and tortured by the police, family and politics. And it also reveals the psychology of family and society also that untouchable and touchable cannot love with each other. As result is well expressed thought Velutha’s words: What the worst thing that can happen? I could lose everything. My job, my family. My livelihood. Everything (p. 334). This harsh and bitter experience reveals reality in her. Like her mother Rahel also suffers from the tortures and mental crisis from her family and society. She is always neglected both in home and society. She becomes the object of sufferance and pity, contempt and hatred. She feels like a fish out of water in the Ayemenem house. She is a girl of rebellion like her mother, Ammu. Rahel is a child of broken home and a daughter of a divorcee-mother, absolutely neglected by the family she is devoid of love and affection that a child is supposed to get during her childhood. Though her mother has a great love for her, but is so helpless due to the cold and indifferent attitude, of the family that she pays a little attention to Rahel. It is the psychology of a child that he/she always wants to get tender love and care from the grown up people. Rahel asks a question to Chacko, she says: Chacko? Rahel said, from her darkened bad, Can I ask you a question? Ask me two, Chacko said. Chacko, do you love Sophie Mol most in the world? She’s my daughter, Chacko said. Rahel considered this Chacko? Is it necessary that people have to love their own children most in the world? (p. 118) Above lines show the psychology of a child who is devoid of parental love. The novelist presents some beautiful episodes in Rahel’s childhood, which clearly shows her rebellious and somewhat abnormal nature. At first, she was blacklisted in Nazarath Convent at the age of eleven when she was caught outside her housemistress’s garden gate decorating a knob of fresh cow dung with small flowers. The next morning she was made to look up the word depravity in the Oxford dictionary. Six months later she was expelled from the school after reported complaints from senior girls. Rahel is extremely polite child. Second, she has no friend. It is to be noted that the abnormalities we see in the character of Rahel is rooted to her past days. It is trauma psychology that makes Rahel a girl of taciturnity, who always wants to lead a life far from the din and bustle of crowded city. It is this psychology that engraves a permanent imprint in the innocent mind of Rahel, who latter on, even develops

an incestuous relation with her brother, Estha. As a matter of fact, human organism has some certain needs, which it wants to get them fulfilled at any cost. Most of the sexual disturbances, psychosomatic diseases, hypertensions and many other such diseases are the result of psychological imbalances. Rahel always keeps herself away from the touch of her relatives because her disdain for them. Rahel occasionally writes to Chacko and Mammachi. But she never returns to Ayemenem. She does not return, when Mammachi died. During this period, she falls, in love with Larry Mc Casline, who was in Delhi collecting material for his doctorial thesis. The novelist observes: Rahel drifted into marriage like a passenger drifts, towards an unoccupied chair in an airport lounge, with a sitting down sense. She returned with him to Boston (p. 18). When Rahel works in an Indian restaurant in New York, she saves a man stabbed to death; this scene adds more fuel to her past memories. In Rahel, the reflection of the novelist is seen. Roy has been the student of Delhi School of Architecture, she was also in love with Goan, a well known architect. In one of the interviews Roy remembers: My boy friend was Goan, he is a very well known architect now, and we hired a little house on beach we used to bake cakes and sell them ....So I left Gerard and come back to Delhi ...there was a whole ground of us in the college who were not particularly welcome in the hostel there—perhaps we were a little too anarchic, (p. 24) As a matter of fact human organism has some certain needs which it wants to get it fulfilled at any cost. In his discussion of traumatic experiences, Freud himself accepts the role of terrifying experiences, which involve danger to life. So, everybody in society wants to protect life from physical injury. This sense of social and personal security develops in the mind of the child as soon as he develops self. William McDougall, a great psychologist rightly holds

the view: Remorse is an emotion which has been commonly regarded by moralists as the most intense of the effects produced by the activity of that peculiar entity ‘the conscience’. It is a complex emotional state implying the existence of a well-developed self- regarding sentiment and, generally, of moral sentiments. It arises upon the recollection of some past action that one deeply regrets; like all regret it is painful owing to the fact that the impulse or desire, which is the root of it and which may be the impulse of anyone of several instincts is directed towards the past rather that towards the future, and is therefore seen to the necessarily and for ever baffled, (p. 136) She hardly went to class. The other students, particularly the boys of the college were also not happy to see RaheTs waywardness and almost fierce lack of ambition. They left her alone. She was also not invited to their nice homes or noisy parties. Even her professors were a little wary of her—her bizarre, impractical building pains, presented on cheap brown paper, her indifference to their passionate critics (p. 18). During her stay at the college hostel, Rahel occasionally wrote to Chacko and Mammachi. But she never returned to Ayemenem. Why? Because she thought that Ayemenem people were quite cool and indifferent to her. She didn’t return when Mammachi died. During this period, she fell in love with Larry McCaslin who was in Delhi collecting material for his doctoral thesis. The novelist observes: Rahel drifted into marriage like a passenger drifts, towards an unoccupied chair in an air port lounge. With a sitting down sense, she returned with him to Boston (p. 18). RaheTs past terrible memories even haunted her happy marriage life. Her husband was very happy to find so good and beautiful girl like Rahel. He held her as though she was a gift, given to him in love. Something still and small. Unbearably precious (p. 19). But one thing always offended him—her eyes which, behaved as though they belonged to some one else (p. 19). He was exasperated because he did not know exactly the meaning of that strange look of Rahel. The novelist beautifully presents the dilemma going on in the mind of Rahel: He didn’t know that in some places, like the country that Rahel came from, various kinds of despair competed for primacy. And that personal despair could never be desperate enough.... What Larry McCaslin saw in RaheTs eyes was not despair at all, but a sort of enforced optimism. And a hollow where Estha’s words had been. He couldn’t be expected to understand that. (pp. 19-20)

Well, their love marriage did not exist for a longtime. Within a few days, Rahel was divorced like her mother Ammu. After the divorce, Rahel worked for a few months as a waitress in an Indian restaurant in New York. She also worked as a night clerk in a bullet proof cabin at a gas station outside Washington where drinkers occasionally vomited into the money tray, and pimps propositioned her with more lucrative job offers (p. 20). She also saw there how a man was mercilessly stabbed to death. This scene again acted like fuel to her past memories. After the divorce Rahel came to Ayemenem like her mother. We notice that she developed a casual attitude to life. She didn’t suffer from the various restrictions imposed by the society. Instead of sighing and sobbing or having a feeling of shame and moral weakness, she startled Comrade Pillai by saying in straightforward way: We are divorced. Rahel hoped to shock him into silence. Divorced? His voice rose to such a high register that it cracked on the question mark. He even pronounced the word as though it were a form of death (p. 130). Thus, we see that Rahel is a loving female character in the novel. Right from her birth, she has been the sufferer of undeserved despair and desolation and has been a victim of the Pappachi moth which tormented every house that he ever lived in. It tormented him his children and his children’s children (p. 49). It is this mental or psychological tortures that makes her an abnormal character that even creates a breach in her merry and jocund marriage life; that makes her rebel student during her school days; that makes her so mad that in a fit of sexual passion, she even goes to the extent of making an illicit or incestuous relation with her own brother, Estha: Only that they held each other dose, long after it was over. Only that what they shared that night was not happiness, but hideous grief (p. 328). The next Mombatti, which draws the attention of the reader, is, Estha, one of the twins of Ammu. Like Rahel, he is also badly tormented and tortured by some past nightmarish experiences: He grew accustomed to the uneasy octopus that lived inside him and squirted its inky tranquillizer on his past (p. 12). He is treated as a lonely waif forsaken by all. He feels himself like a fish out of water in the big Ayemenem House where Baby Kochamma is dead against him and his sister Rahel. She develops a sense of hatred for them. Like his mother, Estha has also not any personal stand in the Ayemenan House. He is like a caged bird that flutters for a free flight in the sky of freedom, innocence and simplicity. But the society is so cruel towards him that it has chained his wings. The first traumatic experience which the sensitive mind of Estha encounters is the misbehaviour of the orange drink lemon drink man in the Abhilash Talkies who forces or rather say, lulls the boy to mastur bate him:

Now if you’ll kindly hold this for me; the Orange drink Lemon drink Man said, handing Estha his penis through his soft white muslin dhoti, I’ll get you your drink. Orange? Lemon? Estha held it because he had to ... so he held a bottle in the one hand and a penis in the other. Hard, hot vein. Not a moon beam. (p. 103) The effect of this traumatic experience, which Estha had in the Abhilash Talkies, is so strong that it sinks deep into the psyche of the seven years old child and haunts him throughout his life. It is a psychological truth that the mind of a child is so sensitive that when his innocence inadvertently comes in contact with experience, it begins to bleed and consequently he is haunted by this nightmarish experience all through his life. And this is what we see in the life of Estha who is seen suffering from a sense of claustrophobia and taciturnity. The second powerful trauma felt by the innocent mind of Estha as well as Rahel is the emotional blackmail collectively webbed by the family, state and administration for betraying an innocent man, Velutha whom Estha loved so dearly. Velutha was under the police custody and was bitterly beaten by the police. It is Baby Kochamma, who seems to be Lady Macbeth in this novel, persuades the twins to betray Velutha in the police station: The Inspector asked his question. Estha’s mouth said, Yes. Childhood tiptoed out. Silence slid in like a bolt. Someone switched off the light and Velutha disappeared (p. 320). In the very beginning of the novel we are told by the narrator how Estha has to lead a miserable life in Calcutta at his father’s residence: how he feels a sense of isolation a quite bubble floating on a sea of noise (p. 11), how at meal times when he wants something, he gets up and helps himself, and how, instead, much to the embarrassment of his father and step-mother, he begins to do the house work. Here, it is noticed that Estha develops a nature of taciturnity and living loneliness. It is all due to the result of brutality and savagery of the Baby Kochamma, Chacko, Mammachi, Inspector Thomas Mathew, etc. It reminds us of an adolescent child Phatik, the central character of the story, The Home Coming by R.N. Tagore. Phatik, the village boy was sent to Calcutta at his maternal uncle’s house where his aunt jeers and insults him without any rhyme or reason; where a silent cry of the inmost heart for the mother, like the lowing of a calf in the twilight (p. 75) is haunted in the heart of this boy, where he dreams night and day of his village home and longs to be back there. Tagore says: The cramped atmosphere and neglect in his aunt’s house oppressed Phatik so much that he felt that he could hardly breathe. He wanted to go out into the open country and fill his

lungs and breathe freely, (pp. 66-67) We notice that when Estha, along with Rahel, goes to Ayemenem House, they become the prey of morbid stiffness. Baby Kochamma reminds the children of their insecure position, of their sinfulness. The reason of her strictness and hypocritical attitude goes to her own repressed sentiment, her failure in love with Father Mulligan. Estha is possessed with such a strange trauma that for him, using a surname is a problem. Why? Because Ammu was uncertain as to whether she should resume her parental title or continue with her husband’s surname. This is why Estha writes Esthapen Unknown. We also see that during the funeral of Sophie Mol, Rahel and Esthapen along with their mother are made to stand separately. Even Kochu Maria, the maidservant of the house does not hesitate to say—These are not your beds. This is not your house (p. 83). Sophie Mol is daughter of Chacko, and she is not as treated as Rahel and Estha. Maragaret Kochamma and Sophie Mol occupy the front seat of the car while Ammu and her children were given back seats. There were also two flasks of water, boiled for Margaret Kochamma and Sophie Mol and tap water for every body else. This step-motherly treatment creates a great hurdle in the life of Estha. K.V. Surendran rightly thinks: For the twins it was darkness, absolute darkness even before they were born. They lived in quietness and emptiness fighting a losing battle. They were born together with a gap of a few minutes, eighteen minutes to be exact. But they were strangers who had met in a chance encounter. But they had known each other before life had begun also barring a few golden moments like the ones they spent with Velutha, they were failing, falling miserable to live like their fellow children, (p. 68) Baby Kochamma is cold and indifferent to Ammu and her twins. Why is it that she is very fond of ornamental garden: the novelist gives the detailed picture of her garden, which symbolically shows the exact nature of Baby Kochamma: Like a lion tamer she tamed twisting vines and nurtured bristling cacti. She limited bonsai plants and pampered rare orchids. She waged war on the weather. She tried to grow edelweiss and Chinese guava. Every night she creamed her feet with real cream and pushed back the cuticles on her toe-nails, (p. 27) The answer of the above-mentioned abnormal attitude which developed in Baby Kochamma’s mind can be properly sought in psychology, particularly in the frustration psychology. Psychology shows that if a man’s ardent desire in his early life is crushed or suppressed, it bursts like lava of volcano in his later life. In other

words, disappointment, frustration of repressed sentiments begins to take its toll in the sufferer’s life. The sufferer’s mind is fractured, with so much psychological maladies that he begins to develop a sadistic attitude so that his long suppressed desires may be compensated. In the case of Mammachi she also manifests trauma and her unsatisfied married life. Mammachi, though not frustrated in love like Baby Kochamma, is an unhappy character in the book. Her marriage life is not peaceful. She is a doll in the hands of her husband, Pappachi, who used to beat her with an iron flower vase, only to show his patriarchal domination over a docile, submissive, ungrudging, un- protesting wife. Her jealousy and hatred for the twins and Velutha can be seen in her unsatisfied quarrelsome marriage life. She, as we shall see, like Baby Kochamma develops an abnormal or neurotic nature in her latter life. Right from the beginning of her marriage life, she has been a silent sufferer. Her husband has a very poor opinion about her. Both the husband and the wife in a happy family should lead a peaceful conjugal life. But it was not in the lot of Mammachi. In the very beginning, the novelist presents a very pathetic picture of her life. She observes: Mammachi was almost blind and always wore dark glasses when she went out of the house. Her tears tickled down from behind them, and trembled along her jaw like raindrops on the edge of a roof. She looked small and ill in her crisps off-white sari. Chacko was Mammachi’s only son. Her own grief grieved her. He devastated her. (p. 5) The frustrated and unsatisfied marriage of Mammachi shows the reader a different tale of woe. Her husband is seventeen years older than she is. He is a respectable and high up man in the society. He is a noted entomologist who has discovered a ‘moth’. But he is a very jealous husband. He is a sadist who wants to fling insult and abuse to his wife without any rhyme or reason, only to get pleasure and nothing else. All these throw morbid impact upon her mind. Ammu, the daughter of Pappachi is always seen remembering those past moments in which Pappachi’s abnormal and embittered conduct made her a great sufferer of the nightmarish experiences unknown to the world of an innocent child. She remembers how her father beats her mother regularly: Every night he beat her with a brass flower vase. The beatings were not new. What was new was only the frequency with which they took place. One night Pappachi broke the bow of Mammachi’s violin and threw it in the river (p. 47). Sadistic behaviour who takes pleasure in tyrannizing his wife and children: Pappachi believes that marriage is the male’s domination or authority over the female. Wife, for him, is only an object, which can be handled

anyway, even an object driven out of their home. Nirmala C. Prakash rightly remarks: In Arundhati Roy’s fictional world man and woman remain only islands and fail to shape up as continents because their relationship lacks mutual love, understanding and adjustment. Pappachi-Mammachi relationship is ridden with jealousy, violence and hatred. Neither the external appearance of Mammachi nor her talent as a successful business woman succeed in ensnaring Pappachi. On the contrary, her flourishing business and growing popularity intensify his jealousy and desire for vengeance. The edifice of their marriage survives but its spirit crumbles totally when Pappachi, warned against beating, withdraws all communication with his wife, (p. 80) Pappachi belongs to such category of man who is not happy to see his own wife flourishing in her art and business. This reflects age old mental framework of traditional husbands. Chacko develops a very cold and indifferent attitude to Ammu, his only sister. Being frustrated in love, he does not want to see Ammu flourishing in the family. He always flings irony on her. He says to Rahel and Estha that Ammu had no Locus Standi (p. 57). Like a domineering and dominating man, he does not want to share the property with Ammu. He says: What is yours is mine and what is mine is also mine (p. 57). This shows how greedy; jealous and self-showing he is! Ammu thinks him a man of the wonderful male chauvinist society (p. 57). When Chacko comes to Ayemenem House after resigning his job as a teacher at the Madras Christian College, he commutes his pension and provident fund to buy a Bharat bottle-sealing machine for the pickle factory. It is he who rehabilitates the factory. Before his arrival, the factory was a small but profitable enterprise. Mammachi ran it like a large kitchen. But Chacko gets the factory registered as a partnership and informs Mammachi that she is the sleeping partner. He invests in equipment like cauldrons cookers, canning machines and expands the labour force. The novelist observes: Though Ammu did as much work in the factory as Chacko, he always referred to in as my factory, my pineapples, my pickles. Legally, this was the case because Ammu, as a daughter, had no claim to the property (p. 57). Margaret Kochamma seeks her identity and wants to be independent. So, she was working as waitress in a cafe in London when at first, she met Chacko. Like Ammu, she left the house of her parents for no greater reason than a youthful assertion of independence (p. 240). She had an ardent desire to be good and gentle lady with enough money. So, she had to face with the ‘real world’. The author points out: “She clung nervously to old remembered rules,

and had no one but herself to rebel against. So even up at Oxford, other than playing her gramophone a little louder than she was permitted at home, she continued to lead the same small, light that she imagined she had escaped” (p. 241). One day, when Chacko came to the cafe, she, like Ammu, all of a sudden, drew towards him. Chacko looked like an untidy beautified Porcupine, he was tall and well built. What attracted her much was Chacko’s shining, happy cheeks and friendly smile. She even shared the uncontrolled laughter with Chacko, a complete stranger: She thought of Chacko’s laugh, and a smile stayed in her eyes for a long time (p. 244). And what Chacko loved most about Margaret Kochamma was her self-sufficiency. He loved the fact that Margaret Kochamma didn’t cling to him. That she was uncertain about her feelings for him. That he never knew till the last day whether or not she would marry him. He was grateful to her for not wanting to look after him for not offering to tidy his room, for not being his cloying mother. He grew to depend on Margaret Kochamma for not depending on him. He adored her for not adoring him (p. 246). Well, both Chacko and Margaret Kochamma were married without their family consent, without their family knowledge. Sophie Mol is the daughter of Margaret Kochamma and Chacko. It is great misfortune for her that when she was an infant, her father was divorced by her mother. So, she was the product of an indifferent and cruel fate. She reminds us of Elizabeth Jane in Hardy’s famous novel, The Mayer of Casterbridge. Henchard deserts (sells out) his beloved wife, Susan in the fair at a time when her wife was pregnant. Sophie Mol has two fathers, one biological who has given her birth and the other ‘real’ who brought her up. Chacko is her biological father divorced at her infancy and Joe was her ‘real’ father killed in a car accident when she was a young child. Sophie Mol has harboured in the core of her heart a sense of isolation. Perhaps this is why she seldom developed love for Chacko. When asked by the twins Who’d you love most in the world? She replied in a very simple way: Joe my dad. She says that Joe is her real father who never hits her. Thus, Roy, genuine describes innocent minds of children like Estha, Rahel and Sophie Mol also. With the help of series of events psychological realities are exposed in The God of Small Thing. I find that no psychoanalysis of any character in literature can be complete and reliable. This is because all the facts, feelings, and experiences that are required for the analysis are never available. Now, in reference to The God of Small Things, it may be urged that Estha is struck silent as a consequence of the sense of guilt. He has not only stopped talking; his mind also appears to have become emptied of any consciousness of the past and the present. Thus in the light of this formulation, the motif of incest will have

to be reinterpreted. Instead of being a psychological aberration, it will have to be thought of as a metaphor for the reunion of the two selves. Roy also shows the psychology of society, which tortures much the persons who totally ruined and disappointed from her own life and thought out their life. 5 Historical Realism Present chapter deals with the historical realism in The God of Small Things. Arundhati Roy picks up entirely different content for her maiden novel in a different style. Even poetry also creeps in her novel. This novel provides her worldwide recognition. Historical realism in The God of Small Things does not in any way run counter to the thematic objectives of the novel. It appears to have been a part of Roy’s intention to cover the bare bones of story with details of social and historical setting and scenario in order to give the reader a feel of patterns of living and daily routine, and sartorial habits, etc. Another significant feature of realistic writing is the description of amusing stock character and activities found in a certain social setting. We have various examples of this kind of sketching. One such character is the ubiquitous old lady who came to help at Sophie MoTs funeral. Masquerading as a distant relative, she often surfaces next to bodies at funerals. She put cologne on a wad of cotton wool and with a devout and gently challenging air dabbed it on Sophie MoTs forehead (p. 5). Although my topic is historical realism in The God of Small Things, social realism will also dwell together. Baby Kochamma herself is something of a stock character with fixed habits and mannerisms. Murlidharn is another example, the level crossing lunatic. He was often seen perched cross-legged on the milestone with an embarrassing posture. R.S. Sharma and S.B. Talwar point out: However, in spite of the author’s sympathy for the poor and dispossessed and identification with them, her portrayal is fragmentary and superficial. It is deflected from its true course by a bourgeois decadent romantic theme. The orientation given to the narrative move away from the true intents of the novel historical and social realism.

Arundhati Roy has provided us so many historical knowledge in terms of human relations. Hence, they are still as untouchable. They grab the disdain and derogative remarks from upper side Christians. They are forced to grapple the atrocities and lead a secluded life. The upper caste Christians avoid having social and marital relations with them. This way of independence brought no relief to them, since they were Christians and therefore no longer belonging to a low Hindu caste, they were deprived of any reservations in any field. But it does not come as a surprise since it has become a fashion in modern Indian writers in English. Arundhati Roy is no exception.
