Certain occurrences tend to become a permanent part of the heritage of a race or community and they are recalled with great fondness by the social group concerned. One such even occurred in 1876 when Baby Kochamma’s father was seven years old. This was the occasion when the Patriach was visiting the Syrian Christians of Kerala. Baby Kochamma’s grandfather had taken his son to the Kalleny house in Cochin to see the Patriarch. They found themselves

right in front of a group of people whom the patriarch was addressing in the verandah. Seizing his opportunity, his father whispered in his young son’s ear which propelled the little fellow forward. The future reverend, skidding on his heels, rigid with fear, applied his terrified lips to the ring on the patriarch’s middle finger, leaving it wet with spit. The patriarch wiped his ring , his sleeve and blessed the little boy. Long after he grew up and became a priest. Reverend Ipe continued to be known as Punnyan Kunju little blessed one and people came down the river in boats all the way from Alleppey and Ernakulam, with children to be blessed by him. The novelist supplies us historical information in sociological terms, that is to say, the social condition of the untouchables in the past. Althought Velutha alone is an active factor in the scheme of the novel, Roy confers us useful historical knowledge in terms of human relations. After the British came to Malabar, a number of low caste people including Velutha’s grandfather, Kelan, become Christians and joined the Anglican Church in the hope of being freed from the curse of untouchability. When converted, they were given some food and money, so they became known as the Rice-Christians. But they soon realized that this did not improve their social position. They were still discriminated against by being given separate churches, separate services and separate Priests. They even had their own Pariah Bishop. In principle, such converts became free of caste discrimination, but in actual social terms, they were still treated as the lowest layer within the Christian community and, as usual, regarded upper caste Christians avoided having social and marital relations with them. The independence brought no relief to them and are segregated. Since they were Christians and therefore no longer belonging to a low Hindu caste, they were deprived of such benefit as job-reservations or bank loans at low interest rates in this historical context that we have to view Vellya Paapen’s worries as regards Velutha’s conduct. Vellya Paapen was an old world paravan and, therefore, he naturally felt that any attempt at social equality on the part of an untouchable would be met with most sever punishment. He had an idea of the practice of backward crawling by the paravans in the past. They happily accepted their history. Their historical realism forced them to follow the path shown by their ancestors. Unlike Velutha’s father she keeps a spark of revolt inside his heart. His statement to Baby Kochamma reflects this. He opposes the blow given by Mammachi and Baby Kochamma telling them Labour Laws. He said that according to the Labour Laws, the days are gone, he told us, when you kick us around like dogs (p. 260). Above lines proves his capability and ability. But his history never let him breath openly. Estha and Rahel were told by Mammachi that she could remember the times when paravans were expected to crawl

backwards with a broom, sweeping away their footprint so that Brahmins or Syrian Christians would not defile themselves by accidentally stepping into a paravan’s foot prints (pp. 73-74). In those days paravans and other untouchables were not allowed to walk on public roads, they could not cover their upper bodies and were forbidden to carry umbrellas. When they spoke, they were required to cover their mouths with their hands so that polluted breath did not reach near the high caste persons they happened to be talking to. Velutha, on the other hand, was a young man of the new age. His manner of talking and dealing with the high caste people had an unmistakable smack of independence, self- respect and social equality. This is what alarmed his father. And it is shown by the consequences that hatred towards paravans and their oppression were still very patient in Kerala. The history of the twins begins with their conception. They are dizygotic twins who differ considerably in physical features and appearance. The twins’ expert who is consulted by the family totally misses the point when he advises that, being dizygotic, they can be separated without any harm. He is not aware that in spiritual terms the two have a single identity: They have two bodies but one soul. Throughout the novel, the differentness of the two is constantly kept in focus and we are informed that when they are reunited after twenty-three years, they look at each-other as strangers. Most of the time the reflecting consciousness is that of Rahel. It is difficult to say why the dissimilarity between Estha and Rahel is so keenly underlined. Is if being used as an argument to say that, where put biology is concerned, sexual relationship between the two is not debarred? We shall return to this issue later. In case of Estha and Rahel Arundhati Roy is much sensitive. She portrays the futures of children whose parents are not with them or have broken relationship. Intercommunity marriage is not accepted by families dominated by old-structure. Roy shows us insecurity, lack of love, humiliation, and isolation, as Rahel is to find later on, Chacko and Mammachi provided the care (food, clothes, fees) but withdrew their concern for her. Even using a name becomes a problem for Estha because Ammu is undecided as to whether she should resume her parental title or continues with her husband’s surname. In this notebook therefore Estha writes Esthappen unknown. To show identity it is necessary to carry father’s surname Rahel and Estha’s acquisition of identity is under confusion. Chacko tells them Ammu has no Locus standi. Their clear break from the family comes when Saphie Mol dies. At her funeral they are allowed to be there but as a segregated part. Roy points out: Though Ammu, Estha and Rahel were allowed to attend the

funeral, they were made to stand separately, not with the rest of the family nobody would look at them. (p. 5) Observing all such instances make Rahel and Estha realize their predicament and battle. Rahel, on the other hand, was wide awake, fiercely vigilant and brittle with exhaustion from her battle against real life. (p. 5) Estha and Rahel witness the quarrels between their mother and father they are tossed from one to the other. When they arrive to live in the Ayemenem house, they becomes a prey to the morbid stiffness and malice of Baby Kochamma, who constantly reminds them of their insecure position, of their ostracization and even sinfulness. The problem of insecurity of the twins in society in very well expressed by the image of the frogs: To Ammu her twins seemed like a pair of small bewildered frogs engrossed in each other’s company, lolloping arm in arms down a high way full of hurtling traffic entirely oblivious of what trucks can do to frogs (p. 43). Both Estha and Rahel are innocent but they are aware of the blatant history. So, they are frustrated and afraid also. They are collecting harsh experiences from their lives. Estha and Rahel learned how history negotiates its terms and collects its due form those who break its laws. They heard its sketching thud. The smelled its smell and never forget it (p. 55). Hence, they are observing all ugly sides of their lives and ready to meet all awards given by history and society. Roy has equitably real off fear, agony, frustration, innocence of children neglected and segregated by family and society. The Christians in Kerala observed untouchability just like the Hindus. The paravan and pulayas joined the Anglican Church to escape the scourge of untouchability (p. 74). The term dalit literally means oppressed section of the society but now the term has attained a wider significance as it refers to the people who are discriminated on the basis of caste and creed. In the past unclean occupations were carried out by the untouchabilities and their presence was considered as a bad omen. It was out of shame that the untouchables were converted to Christianity. The Church and the Christian missionaries played a crucial role in exploiting the pathetic condition of the untouchables. They were made to believe that once they become Christians the caste-stigma would be rubbed off. Initially the dalit Christians received a little money and food as an added incentive. But the newly converted Christians were not given the equal status. The dalit Christians were torn between two worlds one rejected by them and the other not ready to accept them. Mammachi recalls to her memory the rigid caste system that existed in her times:

Paravans were expected to crawl backwards with a broom, sweeping away their footprints so that Brahmins or Syrian Christians would not defile themselves by accidentally stepping into a paravan’s foot print paravans like other untouchables, were not allowed to walk on public roads, not allowed to cover their upper bodies not allowed to carry umbrellas. They had to put their hands over their mouths when they spoke, to divert their polluted breath away from those whom they addressed, (pp. 73-74) Despite being the daughter of upper caste she is ill-behaved by inspector Thomas Mathew. Reason behind this is her relationship with paravan. When this relationship of no future comes in light there is no place lift on the earth to take shelter. He said, Kottayam Police didn’t take statements from Veshya or their illegitimate children (p. 8). This shows historical reality of molestation of such creatures as Ammu, Estha, Rahel, and Velutha. Arundhati Roy also indicates the measure of change that have occurred since the days of Pappachi. In the Nineties anyone who visits a Kerala village will be struck by the contrast between two kinds of house that reflect the disparity between the two sections of people that inhabit them: Other days he walked down the road. Past the new, freshly baked, iced, gulf-money house built by nurses, masons, wire benders and bank clerks who worked hard and unhappily in faraway places. Post the resentful older houses tinged green with envy covering in their private drive ways among their private rubber trees. Each a tottering fiefdom with an epic of its own. (p. 13) The advent of satellite T.V. is shown to have produced considerable impact even on the life style of the older generation. Satellite T.V. became the new love of Baby Kochamma, who was now able to get glimpses of modern life: It wasn’t something that happened gradually. It happened overnight. Blondes, wars, famines, footballs, sex, music, coups d’etat they all arrived on the same train (p. 27). Baby Kochamma enjoyed watching The Bold and The Beautiful and Santa Barbara where brittle blondes with lipstick and hair-styles rigid with spray seduced androids and defended their sexual empires (p. 27). Baby Kochamma was joined by Kochu Maria in pursuing their new hobby, the lady sitting on a chair and the servant on the floor. Finally, it may be noted that realistic fiction often focuses its attention on the seamy and shadowy aspects of life. Description of dirt and filth are generously supplied in The God of Small Things. We are taken to the humble do welling of Velutha where his disabled brother is lying in bed. Even in June of 1993 the river was no more than a

swollen drain, its old, awful grandeur is gone, and now its spirit is spent: It was just a slow, slugging green ribbon lawn that ferried feted garbage to the sea. Bright plastic bags blew across its viscous, weedy surface like subtropical flying-flowers (p. 124). On the other side of the river also, there was filth and dirt produced by the people: Children hung their bottoms over edge and defecated directly onto the squelchy mud of the exposed riverbed. The smaller ones left their dribbling mustard streaks that find their own way eventually, evening, by the river would rouse itself to accept the day’s offering and sludge off to the sea, leaving wavy lines of thick white scum in its wake. Upstream, clean mothers washed clothes and pots in unadulterated factory effluents. People bathed. Severed torsos soaping themselves, arranged like dark busts on a thin, rocking, ribbon lawn. (p. 125) The portrayal of Indian prison speaks real condition of prisoner’s cells at the police stations are notorious for their filth and murkiness. With Estha, we are allowed a glimpse of the pitch dark lock-up in which Velutha was confined. Estha heard the sound of rasping, laboured breathing and the smell of shit made him feel like vomiting. The detailed description of the pickle factory is an excellent piece of realistic writing. It is so detailed and clear because it arises out of Arundhati Roy’s personal experiences. She has herself stated that she spent the early years of her childhood in her grand mother’s factory in Kerala and became a formidable curry-powder packer and pickle label sticker. The factory has gauze doors and the premises are dark and pickle smelling. The barn owl that lived on a blackened beam contributed its droppings to the flavour of certain products. We get a view of the raw materials, products and furniture in the order in which they are placed. Green mangoes, cut and stuffed with turmeric and chilly powder and tied together with twine, glass casks of vinegar with corks, shelves of pectin and preservatives, trays of bitter gourd, gunny bags full of garlic and small onions, heaps of fresh green peppercorns, a heap of banana peels, the label cupboard full of labels, the glue and the glue-brush, an iron tub of empty bottles, the lemon squash and the grape-crush. Roy has amply thrown due light on the class antagonism and exploitation. Let us now turn to a consideration of social realism in the specific sense employed by the Marxist critics. There are clear indications that Arundhati Roy is keenly aware of the exploitation and oppression of the have-nots by the upper classes. In fact, The God of Small Things encompasses the poor, the exploited and the socially rejected people of the Kerala society; they are misfits, outcasts, factory workers, and low caste people. Arundhati Roy projects class

antagonism and class exploitation in terms of caste, and she cleverly makes a contrast between touchable and untouchable. When there is a crucial confrontation, the class affiliations come out in the open. When Velutha is discovered to be carrying on sexual relations with Ammu, all the representatives of the oiling class and its allies form a solid front-the police, the communist leader, the feudal minded elders of the family—all unite in acts of extreme savagery. Arundhati Roy also presents a study of the class character of the C.P.M. leadership. They claim to be part of the working class but in actual fact they are middle class people practicing opportunism and failing to identify themselves with the workers in an act of genuine ‘declassing’—they are for the people, not of them. There is also an attempt to trace the rise of the naxalite movement which seems to enjoy the author’s sympathy. It is also clear that the author has a genuine concern for the downtrodden. She presents a living picture of their suffering and the injustice meted out to them. She is even capable of empathizing with them. In the third chapter, Big Man the Laltain, Small Man the Mombatti she depicts the condition of the Bihari porter. In fact, this chapter symbolically focuses on class antagonism and the meaning of the symbols can be worked out in political and economic terms. Like the laltain, the upper classes are well-fed and well-protected, whereas the lower classes lack security and are subject to the perils of economic and political upheavals. Exposure of Velutha’s love for Ammu destroys his life. He tried to be rational: What’s the worst things that can happen? I could lose every thing. My job my family. My livelihood. Everything (p. 334). It points out that one mistake makes him deprive of all things. This is reality shown by the novelist. He is also jealous of the boy for having a grandmother who owns a pickle factory and for being given pocket money. You’re a lucky rich boy, with pocket money and a grandmother’s factory to inherit, (p. 105) If we psychoanalyze of the man’s child abuse we will discover that the act was a symbolic wish fulfilment for gaining mastery over the upper class. Similarly, if we closely look at Ammu-Velutha relationship, we find that, among other things, what draws Ammu to Velutha is their common discontent against the upper class people. Suddenly Ammu hoped that it had been him that Rahel saw in the march. She hoped it had been him that had raised his flag and knotted arm in anger. She hoped that under his careful cloak of cheerfulness, he housed a living, breathing anger against the smug, ordered world that she so raged against (pp. 175-76). Velutha certainly was aware of the class

antagonism and regarded Ammu and himself as belonging to two opposite camps. He tried to hate her: She’s one of them, he told himself. Just another one of them (p. 214). But the attraction was so strong that he could not maintain his position. He had to jump the class boundary. Most of the portions written with a view to presenting historical reality with special succeed in according verisimilitude to the novel and also add flesh and life to the story. Historical realism, as we have suggested, explains some developments and consequences which would have been regarded as unexpected and unusual in its absence. Most of the realistic material thrown in does not appear to be obtrusive or uncalled for, although some portions like the long description of the pickle factory appear to stand for themselves. However, there are certain matters, political, biographical and personal which do not appear to be well integrated with the theme. However, in spite of the author’s sympathy for the poor and dispossessed and identification with them, portrayal is fragmentary and superficial. It is deflected from its true course by a bourgeois decadent romantic theme. The orientation given to the native moves away from the true intents of the novel of social realism. 6 Social and Gender Discrimination Arundhati Roy’s The God of Small Things is a unique, master-piece novel revealing the truth. Roy considers The God of Small Things as an exposure of life of poor and destitute, weak and helpless, hope and triumph, life and sufferings, all those victimized by tradition’s false pride and esteem. Arundhati Roy has been much successful in depiction of Ammu in compulsive expression of fatal love. As a realist artist the novelist has presented the blatant face of social discrimination. Nothing new is picked out by Roy but every inch reality is exposed. So I cannot fail to describe that throughout her life she has been a literary artist but her social commitment had kindled the spark of activism in her. With immense media support she solved many problems of the people. She tried her best to put her words in the mouth of Ammu and Velutha but at the same time also shows the fatal consequence of the revolt against age old tradition made by men. Ammu’s and Velutha’s failure prove this, despite it, it cannot be described their effort invaluable. Bringing out The God of Small Things she tries to make bridge between the oppressor and the oppressed. K. Ganapathi Reddy presents his view about the celebrity status with activism, “The credibility of Arundhati Roy’s activism stems from the fact that. She has been proactive participant in the socio-environment issues she has emerged as the messiah of popular causes, judiciously mixing her celebrity status with her activism” (2). Along with, Roy also raises the women’s questions regarding their rights and position. Arundhati Roy has projected Ammu as an agent of social reform. Her protagonist raises her voice against her family and struggle to stand on feet. But she never gives her tacit acceptance anywhere, whereas Anita Desai’s protagonists undergo traumatic experiences. Ammu is persecuted by her father, mother and brother because of

their hostile and inclement attitude to her. She is inclined to carve her path on her own rules. But leading female character in Desai’s novel Where Shall We Go This Summer, Sita is never insulted and molested by any other character in the novel. Despite it her conjugal life shatters like that of Ammu because of the wild behaviour of her husband. Sita feels psychological isolation from her husband. Her husband’s pursing of the materialism embarrasses Sita to such a great extent that she never finds emotional support. Anita Desai is also considered as feminist in her novel Fasting Feasting Uma is a meek, doily and passive sufferer. While Ammu is not ready to live her life another’s way, she protests against the age old conventions and rules of ethics. There are many similarities between Ammu’s and Uma’s family atmosphere. Both receive no respect in their families. Both demonstrate the plight of the Indian women. In Uma reflection of Anita Desai is reflected while in Ammu of Arundhati Roy’s. By Roy’s portrayal of Ammu as protagonist she seems to be revolting against the supremacy and high-handedness of patriarchy over matriarchy. Anita Desai is considered as a champion of women. In her novel Fasting Feasting Desai urges freedom of women. There is clear difference between the treatment of women character of Desai and Roy. Whereas Roy’s characters Ammu and Rahel are rebellious sufferers but Desai’s is characters are passive sufferers they learn to live by their suffering. But Ammu is a tragic character who suffers terribly till end her of life. After the dealth of Velutha in the police custody, she leaves Ayemenem House and comes to Alleppy where she meets her tragic death in a hotel named Bharat today. They cause of her tragic end is the mean conspiracy of male members of the community. Roy’s vivid descriptions show her disdain towards the patriarchal dominance of the male section of the society Chacko is a product of patriarchy and members of wonderful chauvinistic society. In this regard Gerda Lerner aptly says: Patriarchy means the manifestation and institutionalization of male dominance over women in society in general (p. 239). In India major concern is discriminating attitude of the parents to their daughter. Uma got no support from her family. Her mother always teaches her recalling her own past days. Since Uma’s mother received no equal behaviour from her parents so it keeps a strong impression upon her conservative mind. Thus Desai projected Uma’s parents as highly conservative, traditional and orthodox in their attitude and outlook. In India various nuts sweets and delicious us are for boys not for girls, while girls need more nourishments than boys. Despite it no attention is paid to them. Uma’s mother way of behaviouring with her children is inherited from her own parents.

Uma and Aruna are differently treated. Uma is not permitted to get education, but is preached to get efficiency in the domestic affairs. Uma’s marital life degenerates into a chaotic life because of her failure in marriage. Her maritial life is reminiscent of Ammu’s frustrated conjugal life. She becomes unhappy in her marriage with an already married man. Anamika is another character who suffered from the tragedy of her worst marital life. Ammu is constantly and regularly beaten by her husband in the same manner as Anamika is beaten by her mother-in-law to the silent and passive witness of her husband. Her condition is much pitiable and worse than animal. She could not think about her own right. The meaning of her life is in the acceptance of the blows provided by her mother-in-laws and husband. This is not the desting of Anamika but of average. Out of many concerns one concern displayed by Arundhati Roy is domestic violence. Mammachi too suffers silently all blows made by Pappachi. In The God of Small Things domestic violence begins with Pappachi’s disappointment in not having been named after the moth he had discovered. Pappachi’s moth was held responsible for his black moods and sudden bouts of temper. Its pernicious ghost... tormented him and his children and his children’s children (49) though Roy would have us believe that in reality he had been ill-tempered long before he discovered the moth. Ammu has been witness of his violence towards his wife. Ammu remembers father bear beat mother bear with a brass vase. Mother bear suffered those beatings with mute resignations (180). Thus, the lives of Mammachi and Pappachi involve an interesting study of domestic violence and anglophilia rolled into one. Chacko avers, they are as a whole a family of anglophiles with an inclination for anything English. Because of the inequality children’s innocence is badly affected. Their healthy development regarding mind and body are restricted. Destroyed childhood is a global crisis. Leela Menon observes, the reports of gen- toting school children in the U.K. Killing and injuring of classmates testify to increasing psychological trauma and social alienation. In contrast, Indian children, are, more victims than offenders. Roy picked out the smallest of the small and shows how She sweet flower of innocence fades when they become victims of adult aggressiveness and cruelty. In the lack of mutual love, understanding and adjustment life cannot pass smoothly and relationship of Pappachi and Mammachi, Ammu and her husband carries no weight. Arrival of Chacko in the Ayemenon House ends Pappachi’s beating. Pappachi never touched Mammachi thereafter. Finding no option to show his frustration he smashed his own favourite chair and smashed it to pieces. All such happenings took place due to his sense of insecurity. Nirmala. C. Prakash sees it, in the

Mammachi-Pappachi relationship, “they remain as island and fail to shape up as continents, because their relationship lacks mutual love, understanding and adjustment” (36). Thus double standards become the norms of this family. Pappachi’s behaviour with others is much decent and gentle and nothing is left to suspension but terrorized his family: He donated money to orphanages and leprosy clinics. He worked hard on his public profile it as a sophisticated generous, moral man. But alone with his wife and children he funned into a monstrous, suspicious bully, with a streak of vicious coming. They were beaten, humiliated and then made to sufferer the every of friends and relations for having such a wonderful husband and father. 7 Conclusion In the foregoing chapters realism and romance have been well discussed in the novel of Arundhati Roy’s The God of Small Things. After all discussion it can be mentioned that realism and romance is highly symbolical in the novel. Most of the portions written with a view to presenting historical and psychological realism in the novel, the novelist has portrayed the socio-political realism of democratic India, where still one community is becoming the victim of the brutality of the majority. The God of Small Things is a story about love, romance, and brutality, the brutality against the dalits. On one hand the human rights and value are globally, seriously considered, on the other hand in rural India this sort of atrocity against dalit are going on. The Ayemenem incident of killing Velutha is the microscopic vision of the orthodoxy’s brutality against dalit. In The God of Small Things various aspects of historical and psychological realism have well reeled off. Social and gender discrimination have been ardently furnished. In the garb of the novel Roy has raised her voice against all accusable burning issues concerning discrimination mentioned above. Very skilfully Roy has indicated the impact of parents in development of children’s personality. It can be conclusively established as a novel of revolt against the social injustice and oppression on women. Roy typifies in the novel as a cruder against these social feature that have built their nests in Indian society. The novel is designed to inculcate a revolutionary idea in the mind of readers and to exert reformative impact on Indian society so as to ameliorate the predicament of women in their domestic and social lives. It also shows the gender discrimination especially between Ammu and his brother Chacko in case of getting education and also shows the caste discrimination

between untouchable and touchable. The God of Small Things clearly shows the untold miseries and undeserved sufferings of women who have to bear the brunt of male domination silently and meekly. Roy has explored issues related to subalternity untouchability, especially the religious hypocrisy, poverty, corrupted system. As a social reformist she presents many illustrations describing the realities embedded in the society. Coming to the novel’s form and technique, it cannot be denied that the subtlety of the plot is something like ‘plotting’ : it certainly overlaps itself with the result that the movement of the story is subject to violent jerks and painful (from the reader’s point of view) movements back and forth. The complicated pattern chosen for the novel also involves excessive repetition which probably accounts for one-fourth of the total volume, at the same time we should not turn a blind eye to certain advantages this formal involution brings with it. The jumping of the narrative from present to past or to future and back in different chapters brings forth a certain amount of pathos and irony, as the case may be, which would have been impossible in a straight narrative. In this connection, we might look again at the last chapter. Before completing it, the reader already knows the subsequent tragic turn of events. The worst that happened is already in our knowledge. But it is precisely against the background of this knowledge that both the pathos and power of love imprint themselves upon our mind, it would, therefore, be wrong to generalize that the staggering of chronological order in the novel is all to its disadvantage. The use of capital letters is a different matter. The God of Small Things, to Summate, is an excellent piece of the exactitude of Arundhati Roy’s recording consciousness. Whatever has been presented in the novel is not part of fiction and imagination only but is keenly observed, deeply felt, realized and carefully constructed in real texture. Use of stream of consciousness technique has made the novel amazingly effective. Constant flashbacks and fast forwards lend a peculiar, cinematographic character to the novel. Everything is presented in organic way. One incident has strong link with other so nothing falls apart from the concerning matter. Roy is an ardent social thinker and her social imagination covers very distinct areas of life. She is also called the princess of prose. In real sense she has mind of social thinker and reformer that has capacity to stir others. Arundhati Roy herself reveals her account: if you’re writer, you tend to keep those aching eyes open. Every day your face is slammed up against the windowpane. Every day you bear witness to the obscenity. Every day you are reminded that there is no such thing as innocence. And every day you have to think of new ways of saying old and obvious things. Things about love and greed. About politics and governance. About

There is no doubt that The God of Small Things is full of merit and a high quality fiction. It has truly depicted the Kerala Society, its political movement, regarded Syrian Christian society with selfishness, obscurantism and intolerable dirtiness and filth. Roy knows the sufferings and injustice in India and naturally sympathizes with dispossessed and suppressed people. An another quality of Arundhati Roy of jumping of the narratives from future to past or rather from present to the past is only to create pathos and irony which is simply not possible in straight simple narrations. Roy used nursery rhymes and many Malayalam words. The language of the novel is fresh and childlike. It is fresh because it has no parallel in the world of fiction. After the detailed discussion it can be concluded that Arundhati Roy is a master of style and technique. Throughout the novel we can see a wonderful use of various literary devices. This is one of technically most accomplished novels to appear in Indian English in recent years, full of innovative flourishes and exuding a continuous urge for experimenting linguistically. It is a mew experience for the readers to go through a world that combines beautifully fact and fiction, here and there, producing an effect that intensifies certain experiences which only she is capable of doing. Satire forms the prominent stylistic element in this novel. The God of Small Things is also significant for its apt use of symbolism. Roy’s similes excel her plot construction, her characterization and above all, her truthful portrayal of the social indiscrimination. The God of Small Things is highly symbolic as the matter of fact of style and technique. Having gone through The God of Small Things many themes comes forth before us; class division and castiest oppression lie at the heart of it but there are also many illustrations which are sufficient to caste the feministic impression. It is well manifested how the lives of Indian women are distorted due to so age -old conventions. Rebellion against patriarchy does not meet the fruition. In the present novel there is feminist rebellion against patriarchy and political satire against Marxism. Ammu and Velutha are main victims, they are victimized by the force of history, conventions of respectability, social taboos and politics of opportunism. Being low caste creature Velutha’s entrance in the life of Ammu is partial, not complete. It is much clear from Ammu’s Dream. In her dream Velutha appears one armed. If he kissed

her he could not see her, if he saw her he could not feel her refers to Velutha’s low birth which doesn’t allow him to appear in her dream, love and life. Estha and Rahel are also sufferers. The twins are condemned for being the children of a divorcee who came back to her paternal home. This was a shocking event for the members living in the Ayemenem House. The betrayal of a loved one Velutha destroys Estha and her mental peace completely. Estha becomes speechless because of his sense of the guilt. His silence is more powerful than all the screams of the other characters. In The God of Small Things one is very clear that men’s multi- faced and complex nature is revealed from the pen of a female writer. Roy has depicted the atrocities, brutalities, discrimination, aberration and hardships undertaken by women. In this connection men are the victimizers and women as victims. The novelist is not inclined to see and present only, pleasant sight of the life and world but more precisely described things in as bare way as they are. She moves a little further among women writers to portray brutalities of different kinds in her most admired fiction. Velutha and Estha are victims of crimes committed by men to men. Roy did not manifest both reactions explicitly. In the novelist elaborate raving we are confronted with various kinds from social to personal or psychological. Most of crimes committed are those by men or women who themselves are trying to live in a society which had established certain unspoken, unwritten laws or those that family wants all to accept, because everyone is afraid, either of social ostracism or other fears which are much personal in nature. Thus she shows her excellent talent in describing the universal problems. If men are flower, women are essence. Without women’s contribution there will be no charm and colour in the life and imagination of the universe cannot be. Nari is considered Shakti from Indian accounts then why is so powerless before such creature who is made of her? It is nothing but opportunity which makes man stronger than woman. Age-old laws should be changed observing the demand of time. Roy popularized South Asian fiction in 1997 when The God of Small Things became on international sensation. Roy insisted from the beginning that she was no more influenced by Salman Rushdie, but it is difficult to see how she could have avoided his influence, pervasive among younger South Asian writers. Particularly notable here are such typically Rushdie’s stylistic tricks as capitalizing significant words and running together other words. More importantly, her novel is filled with the same sort of insistent foreshadowing as occurs throughout Midnight Children, and like Rushdie uses in incongruously jaunty tone to relate tales of horror and tragedy, like his Same, Roy’s novel is partly a protest against south

Asian prudery, that stands in the way of love. However, as time passed, readers began to notice the significant difference between Rushdie and Roy. Roy’s novel is much easier to read than most of Rushdie’s works. Although her prose is rich and intricate, it is hardly obscure. Her strongest point is the depiction of children and their view of the world. Women generally dominate the novel’s foreground, with men in supporting roles. Several of the male characters are abusive, and Estha and Velutha are ineffectual victims. Roy’s novel was rich enough to beat out Rushdie himself for the 1997 Booker Prize. It was also captivating enough to become a favourite with millions of enthusiastic readers unwilling to work their way’s through Rushdie’s more challenging prose. The God of Small Things is a post colonial representation where the order and metaphorical function of home or domesticity is radically called into questions. The God of Small Things gives the massage to readers that women are suffered much in the male dominated society for their rights and this problem is also present in our society that women are ill-treated. Thus, it can be clearly seen that The God of Small Things is highly symbolical on the point of view of historical and psychological realism. Certainly, The God of Small Things has taken Arundhati Roy to greater heights and glorious achievement in Indian fiction in India. On the basis of her achievement and popularity she is considered a frank novelist and activist. The subject of her focus has been poor class people (deserted). Their problems and predicament are accommodated in her works in a different way. Inner self of downtrodden and women (especially divorced) are delved out by her pen in The God of Small Things.
